item.title: Trump official seeks $50 billion for air traffic control after outage
item.description:
USA-AVIATION/

The Trump administration boosted its request for air traffic control funding to $50 billion late Friday after a communications issue forced a nationwide groundstop that halted thousands of flights for hours.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the White House earlier on Friday asked for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system.

"This is an emergency," Duffy said. "What's more important than having an air traffic control system that actually works?"

The issue impacted the FAA's en route centers that handle traffic between airports. But the Republican-led Senate Commerce Committee said the incident highlights the need to prioritise modernising those centers over other projects and noted Congress approved $1.9 billion to replace outdated en route centers.

The world's most complex airspace has experienced a series of events in recent years that have disrupted flights and risked safety. In January 2025, a midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people.

Congress already approved $12.5 billion over five years in July 2025 to upgrade air traffic control and increase the hiring of controllers following complaints about airport ​congestion, flight delays and technology ​problems.

The request from White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy seeks $10.1 billion for air traffic control modernization, including $7.2 billion for a common automation platform and controller workstations and $2 billion for cloud computing.

"This investment is critical to complete the modernisation of our national airspace - delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure," Duffy and Vought wrote to lawmakers asking for swift action.

Major airlines including American Airlines AAL.O, Delta Air Lines DAL.N, United Airlines UAL.O and Southwest Airlines LUV.N have expressed support for the request.

The $30.1 billion request also includes $2 billion to replace and improve Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control towers and $18 billion for airport-related projects including $10 billion to modernise or replace aging terminals.

The FAA relies on decades-old ​computers as well as replacement parts bought through auction websites. Last week, it said it would replace by the end of 2028 floppy disks used for weather and other critical information at more than 400 air traffic control facilities.

Vought and Duffy in their letter said the FAA has replaced 68 per cent of legacy copper telecommunications network with high-speed fiber infrastructure.

The administration has called for the Republican-led Congress to approve funding in the final weeks of the year. Democrats are set to take control of Congress in January.

In September, the dual failures of a circuit at a Philadelphia ​air traffic facility and the ​accidental severing of a ⁠fiber-optic cable in New Jersey by a construction crew led to thousands of flights across the densely populated Northeast being delayed or canceled.

item.title: Trump, Xi, Putin to hold historic meeting in China, what’s on the agenda
item.description:
APEC-SUMMIT/TRILATERAL-MEETING

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping will hold the first ever three-way meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China at a summit in Shenzhen next week, the White House said Friday.

Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, US officials said.

The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.

One of the major conflicts dominating Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the US officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that US envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.

Tesla and Space X boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but won't be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.

Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday , their fourth meeting since the US president's return to power last year.

But Trump is not scheduled to have a separate one-on-one with Putin.

Among other topics, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy is not expected to come up in Trump's meetings with Xi, the officials said.

"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," a second US senior official said.

The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.

Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit before heading to Shenzhen.

Fifth shipment of uranium arrives at Rooppur plant
item.description:
The fifth shipment of uranium fuel for the second unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Pabna arrived at the project site early Saturday, marking another step towards the plant's commissioning.
The fuel, sourced from Russia, was transported to the plant in three specialised lorries at around 5:30am under tight security.
Members of the Bangladesh Army and other law enforcement agencies provided security during the transportation.
According to project sources, six shipments of uranium fuel have reached the site so far: one for the first unit and five for the second unit.
Under the delivery plan drawn up by Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, 163 uranium fuel assemblies are scheduled to be delivered for the second unit through seven cargo flights. Another 48 assemblies are planned to arrive in two separate cargo shipments as reserve fuel for the first unit. This will bring the total number of shipments to nine.
Meanwhile, preparations for commissioning the plant's first unit are also underway. The unit is currently in the "Power Start-up Stage-C" phase, for which the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) Chairman granted approval on October 29.
During this phase, the reactor's power output will be gradually increased to test the performance of various plant components, including turbines, generators and safety systems.
Once the tests are completed successfully, the generator of the first unit will be connected to the national power grid in a process known as synchronization.
According to the project plan, the first unit is expected to supply around 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid on a trial basis in November. However, the start of trial power generation will depend on the completion of the necessary tests and approval from the regulatory authority.
Built with Russian technology, the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant comprises two units equipped with VVER-1200 reactors. Once fully operational, the plant is expected to significantly boost the country's power generation capacity and strengthen long-term energy security.

item.title: Climate pledges fall short as Bangladesh seeks $11bn annually
item.description:
Bangladesh has urged developed countries to accelerate climate finance delivery, saying it needs between $10 billion and $11 billion annually to address the impacts of climate change, as international funding commitments continue to fall short of the needs of vulnerable nations.
The country is already spending an estimated $4.5 billion to $5 billion annually from domestic sources on climate-related initiatives, highlighting the scale of investment required to strengthen resilience and support its transition to a lower-carbon economy.
The demand was raised at a press briefing by the Bangladesh delegation on Thursday during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where climate finance remains a central issue in negotiations between developed and developing countries.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo said the progress made in pledging climate finance had not been matched by the actual delivery of funds.
The delegation called for more accessible international financing, particularly grant-based support, arguing that complex approval procedures and delays in disbursement were preventing vulnerable countries from responding effectively to climate risks.
Foreign Affairs State Minister Shama Obaed Islam stressed that financial assistance must reach communities facing the greatest climate threats rather than remain tied up in lengthy funding processes.
Responding to a question from Carbon Brief about Bangladesh's expectations from the climate finance work programme, a delegation representative said greater clarity was needed on funding responsibilities and distribution mechanisms.
The representative also highlighted the challenges facing communities displaced by river erosion, underscoring the need for financing arrangements that can respond to the immediate needs of climate-affected populations.
Bangladesh's demands reflect broader concerns among least developed countries (LDCs) over the widening gap between climate finance commitments and the resources available to implement adaptation measures.
In its written statement, the delegation backed the LDC Group's call for a threefold increase in adaptation finance to $120 billion annually before 2035.
It urged developed countries to meet their existing climate finance commitments and expand grant-based assistance, particularly to support the implementation of National Adaptation Plans in climate-vulnerable countries.
Bangladesh also called for simplified and more direct access to the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Adaptation Fund.
The delegation supported an LDC proposal to establish a platform connecting national adaptation priorities with potential funders and development partners, aiming to bridge the gap between countries' climate plans and their implementation.
On the Global Goal on Adaptation, Bangladesh said the proposed Belém Adaptation Indicators should provide a meaningful way to measure progress in climate resilience without introducing additional reporting requirements for developing countries.
It also called for greater financial and technical support for locally led adaptation, recognising the importance of community-level initiatives in responding to climate impacts.
Bangladesh raised concerns over the limited resources available to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, saying its existing financing was insufficient to meet demand from submitted proposals.
The delegation called for increased financial contributions, simplified direct-access arrangements and faster disbursement to countries experiencing the consequences of climate change.
It also stressed that funding should address both economic losses, such as damage to infrastructure and livelihoods, and non-economic losses, including displacement and damage to cultural and social assets.
The written statement further said Bangladesh was among the first five countries expected to receive $30 million each from the Climate Investment Funds.
Coastal infrastructure and climate-resilient agriculture were identified as priority areas for the expected financing.
The delegation also raised concerns over unilateral climate-related trade measures, including the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
It warned that such measures could place additional pressure on businesses, workers and exporters in developing countries, potentially undermining their economic development efforts.
Responding to questions about whether the issue should feature in a COP31 decision, a delegation representative argued that countries that had benefited from activities contributing to the climate crisis should also take responsibility for supporting those most affected.
The representative said climate policies should not create additional trade barriers for developing economies already facing the costs of climate impacts and the transition to cleaner production.
Journalists also questioned whether COP negotiations included dedicated financing to protect children and safeguard their education in climate-vulnerable countries.
A delegation representative said they were not aware of any specific financing demand exclusively dedicated to children, while referring to ongoing efforts to strengthen healthcare services.
On the broader question of benefits for vulnerable communities, the delegation said international negotiations had helped establish climate change as a shared global challenge and encouraged countries to develop action plans, although implementation remained a major challenge.
Bangladesh accounts for less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions but has reaffirmed its commitment to reducing emissions under its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).
The country has pledged to reduce emissions by 6.39% below its business-as-usual projection by 2035 using domestic efforts, with a further 13.92% reduction conditional on receiving international support.
The delegation backed extending the Mitigation Work Programme through 2030, calling for sector-specific action supported by adequate financing, technology transfer and capacity-building.
It also stressed that the transition to a low-carbon economy must be just and inclusive, prioritising least developed and other climate-vulnerable countries while protecting employment, expanding skills development and providing social protection for affected workers and communities.
Bangladesh said it would continue coordinating with the LDC Group, the G77 and China, and other international partners during the second week of COP31 to push for stronger outcomes on climate finance.
For Dhaka, the central challenge is no longer simply securing new financial pledges but ensuring that promised resources reach countries and communities facing the consequences of a crisis they have contributed relatively little to creating.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: Dhaka ranks world's third most polluted city Saturday morning
item.description:
Dhaka, the densely populated capital of Bangladesh, ranked third among the world’s most polluted cities on Saturday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 195 at 9:14am.
The city’s air was classified as "unhealthy", indicating a health threat, according to the AQI report.
India’s Delhi, Pakistan’s Lahore and India’s Kolkata occupied the first, second, and fourth spots on the list, with AQI scores of 235, 232, and 192, respectively.
According to the AQI scale, a reading between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate", with generally acceptable air quality, though sensitive individuals should limit prolonged outdoor exertion. AQI levels of 101–150 are "unhealthy for sensitive groups", 151–200 is "unhealthy", 201–300 is "very unhealthy", and readings above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing severe health risks.
The AQI, which reports daily air quality, informs residents how clean or polluted the air is and highlights potential health effects. In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution. Air quality usually deteriorates in winter and improves during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that air pollution causes about seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: UN climate chief urges debt-free climate finance for developing nations
item.description:
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has called for a fundamental shift in the global climate finance system, urging developed countries, financial institutions and investors to ensure that funding helps developing nations escape mounting debt pressures and build long-term economic resilience.
Speaking at the Seventh Biennial High-Level Ministerial Dialogue on Climate Finance at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday, Stiell warned that many developing countries remain trapped in a cycle of debt, climate disasters and increasingly expensive borrowing, leaving them with fewer resources to protect their people and economies.
“Climate finance must help countries break free,” he said, stressing that meeting international funding targets alone would not necessarily address the actual financial needs of vulnerable nations.
He argued that climate finance must move beyond funding individual projects towards supporting broader economic transformation, strengthening national institutions and creating conditions that attract more investment at lower costs.
Under the new climate finance goals agreed at COP29, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing $300 billion annually by 2035, while all actors are expected to work together to scale up financing for developing countries from all sources to $1.3 trillion per year by the same year.
Stiell said the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap provides a pathway towards achieving these targets, but stressed that the way climate finance is delivered must change to make the commitments meaningful.
Explaining the financial challenges facing developing countries, Stiell said the growing threat of floods, wildfires, storms and droughts increases borrowing costs even before disasters occur.
When climate shocks strike, government revenues decline while recovery and reconstruction expenses rise, pushing countries further into debt.
This leaves governments with fewer resources to invest in climate adaptation, resilience and low-emission development, reinforcing a cycle of financial vulnerability.
To break this cycle, he called for climate finance that reflects individual countries' economic circumstances and debt sustainability.
He emphasised that funding must be affordable and tailored to national needs rather than delivered through a one-size-fits-all approach.
While private finance, loans and guarantees remain important for meeting global climate goals, he said grants and highly concessional financing would continue to be essential, particularly for least developed countries (LDCs), small island developing states (SIDS) and other vulnerable economies.
He also called for broader international efforts to address debt burdens so that developing countries are not forced to choose between repaying loans and investing in climate resilience.
Stiell identified easier access to climate finance as another major priority, pointing to the complicated administrative requirements and fragmented funding arrangements that developing countries must navigate.
He said countries often face complex procedures to access funding from multiple programmes and institutions, making it difficult to secure resources when they are needed.
“We need procedures simplified,” he said, calling for stronger coordination among financial institutions and reduced administrative burdens.
He also stressed that international climate finance should align with national development priorities rather than requiring countries to reshape their domestic systems to meet external funding requirements.
National treasuries, local governments, development banks and financial institutions already play important roles in financing development, and these institutions should be strengthened rather than bypassed, he said.
Stiell urged international partners to invest in institutional capacity and help developing countries establish effective systems to access, manage and deploy climate finance.
He also underscored the importance of developing and transferring technologies that support climate-resilient and low-emission development.
The UN climate chief further called for stronger cooperation among governments, climate funds, development banks, financial institutions and private investors to turn national climate plans into tangible investments.
He said climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building must work together around countries' own priorities, ensuring that funding translates into projects that strengthen resilience and improve people's lives.
As an example, he explained that early grant-based support could help countries build institutional capacity and develop investment pipelines, while concessional finance and risk-sharing instruments could subsequently help projects expand.
He said international climate negotiations and cooperation mechanisms could play an important role in bringing different sources of finance together around national development priorities.
Concluding his remarks, Stiell called for a new approach to international climate finance, saying the biennial ministerial dialogues should help translate commitments into more effective delivery.
Established in 2013, the dialogues have contributed to discussions on global climate finance. However, he said they must now help advance a system that supports long-term development rather than focusing solely on individual funding targets.
“Where every dollar invested in development builds a better future. For all countries,” he said.
His remarks at COP31 highlight a central challenge for developing countries such as Bangladesh: securing not only greater volumes of climate finance but also affordable, accessible and predictable funding that can strengthen economic resilience without deepening existing debt pressures.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: Pretext being created for unreasonable wage announcement: BGMEA president
item.description:
BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan has alleged that an anarchic situation is being created to pave the way for an irrational wage announcement.

The BGMEA President said, “The wage board was formed on 1 November. The chaotic situation began in the last week of October. If we consider what happened last month as logical, then what is happening now is not logical at all. The wage board has already been formed.”

He further stated, “The most crucial matter—when the increased wages will be effective—was announced at the very first meeting of the board. Despite this, creating an anarchic situation means setting the stage for an irrational wage announcement under pressure.”

BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said these things in response to a journalist's question at a joint press briefing of the two organisations of garment industry owners—BGMEA and BKMEA.

The press conference held at the BGMEA complex in Uttara on Saturday afternoon was attended by BKMEA Executive President Fazle Shamim Ehsan, Vice President Amal Poddar, BGMEA Vice President Rezwan Selim, Mizanur Rahman, among others.

Referring to the ongoing unrest, BGMEA President, in a written statement, mentioned that 147 factories in Savar-Ashulia and Gazipur are unable to continue production activities despite efforts, due to the disruption in overall security and favourable production environment. If the factories fail to carry out production activities due to ongoing labour unrest, they will be forced to close from tomorrow under Section 13 (1) of the labour law.

The BGMEA President said that 55 factories in Savar-Ashulia and Gazipur were closed indefinitely under Section 13 (1) today, Saturday.

However, 92 factories tried but failed to resume production. These factories were compelled to grant leave.

In response to a question, the BGMEA President said, “According to labour law, there is no provision to close factories under Section 13 (1) whose operations are ongoing and can conduct regular production. However, those unable to do so, wherever they might be, have that right.”

Mahmud Hasan Khan revealed that BGMEA and BKMEA have tried to keep the factories running at their request until now. Although production started every morning, it couldn’t continue for more than an hour. Therefore, they have the legal right to do so.

In response to another question, Mahmud Hasan Khan said it is not possible for BGMEA to identify who is creating chaos. Law enforcement agencies are working on this. Those who are creating this anarchic situation are already within the network of law enforcement agencies.

On Saturday morning, a joint consultation meeting of BGMEA and BKMEA members was held at the BGMEA auditorium. More than a thousand garment factory owners participated.

In the consultation meeting, the BGMEA President, expressing the members' opinions, said, “They strongly stated that it is questionable to discuss wages at the wage board when vandalism occurs at factories and roads are blocked. However, as responsible members of society, we will participate in the wage board’s third meeting on 16 November. We hope that the situation will improve in the next 1–2 days. If it continues, we will sit again to decide.”

The BGMEA President accused the labour unions of not playing an effective role in stopping the chaotic situation.

He said many grassroots leaders, activists, and worker representatives are unable to maintain control over the common workers, complicating the overall situation further.

Later, in response to a journalist's question, Mahmud Hasan Khan said, “Those who work for labour rights have members in factories even if there is no trade union in every factory. We expect that members of labour federations in these factories will play a role to prevent an anarchic situation. If the minimum wage board is not allowed to work peacefully, if we remain busy on the streets in this chaotic situation, if labour leaders are also busy on the streets, how will they propose a fair wage?”

item.title: Shahjalal Airport's third terminal to partially open on 16 December
item.description:
The government plans to partially open the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka on 16 December. Initially, the terminal will begin operations with four flights.

Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat announced this at a meeting on preparations for the inauguration and operation of the third terminal at the conference room of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) on Saturday morning.

At the meeting, the minister said opening the third terminal was an important commitment of the current government.

The prime minister’s directives must be given the highest priority to ensure that operations begin on schedule. All relevant agencies must complete their respective tasks within the stipulated timeframe.

The meeting discussed various issues, including the activation of the required immigration booths before the terminal opens, installation of baggage belts and scanners, trial operations and signing of agreements.

Representatives of the relevant agencies exchanged views on progress and identified the steps needed to complete the remaining work.

M Rashiduzzaman Millat said the collective efforts of all concerned over a long period had brought the third terminal to the stage where it was ready to begin operations.

He urged the relevant agencies to implement the decisions taken at the meeting on time.

Among those present were Invest Bangladesh Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, Dhaka-18 MP SM Jahangir Hossain, Prime Minister’s Special Assistant Gias Uddin, Civil Aviation and Tourism Ministry Secretary Nurunnahar Chowdhury, and National Board of Revenue Chairman Ahsan Habib.

item.title: Titumir: Forensic audit finds overestimated GDP figures since 2014-15
item.description:
Bangladesh's GDP estimates were overstated by 0.8 to 1.13 percentage points, particularly since fiscal year 2014-15, due to alleged manipulation of data across seven economic sectors under the previous government, Prime Minister's Adviser on Finance and Planning Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir said on Saturday.
Speaking at a seminar on the peer review of a draft forensic audit report at the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), Titumir said the review identified inconsistencies in 22 industrial subsectors, particularly where estimates relied on administrative and secondary data rather than field surveys.
He alleged that economic statistics had been manipulated to present an exaggerated picture of growth and promote a political development narrative.
The review found discrepancies in cement production and value addition, as well as unusual fluctuations in petroleum-sector data. It also identified inconsistencies among export figures maintained by the Export Promotion Bureau, Customs and Bangladesh Bank.
Titumir said the government had decided to use actual Bangladesh Bank data for export-related calculations to address these discrepancies. He added that the review excluded exceptional statistical outliers, including the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic.
The adviser said the government was working to establish a politically neutral statistical system whose credibility would not change with a change of administration.
Measures include introducing computer-assisted personal interviews to improve field-level data collection, verifying GDP estimates against electricity and gas consumption, and improving industrial-sector sampling methods.
The government is also considering quarterly GDP estimates, an income-based approach to national accounting and an open-data policy to give researchers and the public wider access to official statistics.
Bangladesh Economic Association Convener Prof Mahbub Ullah stressed the need for stronger field-level data collection, particularly in agriculture and the informal economy, to improve the accuracy of national accounts. He also called for scientifically representative samples and greater adherence to the UN System of National Accounts.
The seminar was attended by economists, statisticians and researchers, with keynote papers presented by Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies Director General Dr A K Enamul Haque and Dhaka University Professor Dr Atonu Rabbani.

item.title: Law minister: Legal process complete for Hasina’s return, India to decide
item.description:
The government has completed all necessary legal procedures to bring back former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who was sentenced to death in a crimes against humanity case related to the 2024 uprising.
Her return now depends on a decision by the Indian government, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka on Saturday.
Asked about Hasina's possible return and the legal steps involved, the minister said Bangladesh had completed the required procedures and the matter was now in India's hands.
On whether Hasina would have an opportunity to appeal, Asaduzzaman said she would not be entitled to do so under the law enacted by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
The minister also said the investigation agency and prosecution would soon begin investigations into crimes against humanity in different districts, adding that the government would provide all necessary support.
Regarding the investigation into bringing the Awami League to trial as a political party, he said the government would not interfere in the process.
The investigation agency and prosecution would be allowed to carry out their duties independently, he added.

item.title: Import costs rise; LC openings surge 25% in four months
item.description:
Rising global prices for fuel and various other commodities are driving up import costs.
During the first four months of the current FY27 (July–October), letters of credit (LCs) opened for merchandise imports totaled $29.78 billion—a 25% increase compared to the same period of the previous fiscal year.
Over the same timeframe, LC settlements grew by 11.38%.
As a result, demand for the US dollar in the foreign exchange market is rising, pushing exchange rates upward.
According to Bangladesh Bank data, LC settlements during the first four months of the current FY27 reached $24.86 billion, while export earnings stood at $17.04 billion.
This resulted in a merchandise trade deficit of $7.82 billion.
During the first three months, this deficit stood at $7.47 billion.
Meanwhile, expatriate workers remitted $1.146 billion during the same period, representing a 12.97% increase compared to the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.
Data shows that LCs worth $7.32 billion were opened in October, compared to $8.52 billion in the previous month of September.
LC settlements in October amounted to $5.95 billion, down from $6.45 billion in September.
Settlement amounts in July and August stood at $6.28 billion and $6.19 billion, respectively.
Bankers note that although remittances and export earnings are growing, strong demand for US dollars across various sectors—particularly for settling import liabilities—is driving up the exchange rate.
On Thursday, the US dollar traded at a maximum of Tk124.75 in the interbank market, with an average rate of Tk124.65, compared to an average of Tk 124.42 the previous day.
At the beginning of October, the dollar rate was Tk123. It then climbed steadily, reaching Tk123.99 by the final working day of the month.
Meanwhile, to ease pressure on the foreign exchange market, Bangladesh Bank recently sold $222 million to several commercial banks, which also caused foreign currency reserves to decline.
Gross reserves had surpassed $37 billion by the end of June 29, and rose to $37.85 billion in the first week of July.
Reserves on Thursday dropped to $34.99 billion. According to the IMF's BPM6 international accounting standard, reserves currently stand at $30.13 billion.
Comprehensive import data from Bangladesh Bank is not yet available. However, figures for the first three months indicate a substantial increase in fuel import expenses.
During this period, expenditure on petroleum product imports reached $4.22 billion—a 105% increase compared to the same period of the previous fiscal year.
Consumer goods import costs rose by 26.50% to $1.40 billion.
Conversely, imports of capital machinery decreased by 13.60%.
To maintain a stable supply of essential food items and keep prices under control ahead of the upcoming Ramadan, Bangladesh Bank has allowed importers to open usance (deferred payment) LCs with terms of up to 90 days for 10 types of commodities.
Under this facility, importers can pay for the goods within the stipulated period after receiving them.
The list of special items includes rice, wheat or flour, onions, lentils, edible oil, sugar, chana (gram), peas, spices, and dates.
These commodities can be imported under suppliers' credit or buyers' credit.
Previously, the central bank had instructed that LC margins for importing these commodities be kept at a minimum level.

item.title: Report: Banks lacking capital to absorb losses as NPLs hit 32.78%
item.description:
The default loan rate in Bangladesh's banking sector has surged to 32.78%. This means nearly one-third of all disbursed loans in the banking sector are now non-performing (defaulted).
Furthermore, there is virtually zero likelihood of recovering 80% to 90% of these defaulted loans.
Compounding the crisis, banks lack the necessary capital to absorb the losses stemming from these defaulted loans. By the end of 2025, the banking sector’s capital conservation ratio stood at a negative 2.64%.
As a result, the country's banking sector is under severe pressure from a dual crisis of high default rates and capital deficits.
These findings were revealed on Saturday (November 14) at a Knowledge Hub Institute seminar in Dhaka titled “Banking Sector Evaluation and Policy Review: January–September 2026.”
The report was presented by Noor Iyana Jannat, research associate at the institute.
Knowledge Hub president Khondaker Golam Moazzem and other board of trustee members were present at the event.
According to a KHI report, the capital situation of the banking sector is equally alarming. At the close of 2025, the capital conservation ratio was negative 2.64%, with a provisioning shortfall of approximately Tk191,441 crore.
Additionally, court injunctions on 845 pending lawsuits have blocked the recovery of Tk182,419 crore.
Shah Md Ahsan Habib, component lead at Knowledge Hub, remarked that the volume of default loans is extraordinary.
"Nearly one-third of all disbursed loans cannot be recovered. Even worse, the overall capital of the banking sector is negative, meaning there is a severe deficit in the capital required to absorb loan-related losses."
Analyzing the classification of NPLs, he noted that a large portion falls into the doubtful and bad loan categories. Specifically, for bad loans, the chance of recovery is virtually non-existent—accounting for roughly 80% to 90% of all defaulted loans.
"My personal assessment is that less than 10% of this 33% default rate stems from genuine credit risk," Habib stated.
"The vast majority is tied to operational risk, procedural irregularities, and criminal offenses. Tackling these crimes is beyond the capacity of banks alone; the government and the central bank must step in."
Impact of willful defaulters
Highlighting the issue of willful loan defaults, Habib noted that a significant portion of NPLs results from deliberate evasion—a fact recognized by regulators and market insiders alike.
"Ordinary depositors are bearing the cost of willful defaults," he warned. "Many bank employees who were never involved in the loan disbursement process are also paying the price. Honest businesses are forced to borrow at higher interest rates, and even sound banks are absorbing the shockwaves. Ultimately, the entire economy is bearing the cost because our financial system is heavily bank-dependent."
The report highlighted sharp disparities in default rates across different categories of banks:
Meanwhile, while overall deposits grew, credit growth in the private sector slowed.
Deposit growth in the banking sector reached 11.96% in August, while private sector credit growth crawled at just 4.75% during the same period, dropping further to 4.09% in September.
In September, inflation stood at 8.34%, and the policy interest rate was maintained at 9.50%. Foreign exchange reserves stood at $31.20 billion on September 30. Remittance growth reached 13.28% between July and September.
Although excess liquidity in banks stood at Tk441,954 crore in August, the report cautioned that aggregate excess liquidity can mask severe crises in weaker, vulnerable banks.
To navigate the crisis, the report recommends conducting independent loan reviews of vulnerable banks by December, and establishing bank-specific capital recovery or resolution frameworks by March 2027.
It also stressed the importance of regular public disclosures regarding cash recoveries, capital adequacy, and customer service quality.
The report touched upon the Bank Resolution Act 2026, the Deposit Protection Act 2026, and the Tk35,000 crore capital restructuring package announced for Sammilito Islami Bank.
However, it noted that concrete evidence of completed payout mechanisms for depositors in the merged bank has yet to be observed.

item.title: Up to Tk50 lakh grants for startups
item.description:
The government is set to provide grants of up to Tk50 lakh to startup companies to foster innovation-based new entrepreneurs and develop technology-driven businesses in the country.
Along with Bangladeshi citizens, non-resident Bangladeshis (NRBs) will also be eligible to apply for these grants.
To facilitate this, the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Division has formulated the "Information and Communication Technology Related Startup Grant Management and Operation Policy, 2026."
According to the policy, grants ranging from Tk1 lakh to Tk50 lakh will be disbursed depending on the various stages of a startup's development.
Grants of Tk1 lakh to Tk3 lakh will be allocated for idea development, Tk3 lakh to Tk10 lakh for prototypes and Minimum Viable Products (MVPs), and Tk10 lakh to Tk30 lakh for investment readiness, bridge, and matching funding.
However, considering justification and special circumstances, the grant amount can reach up to Tk50 lakh.
Individual applicants at the prototype and MVP stages can receive up to Tk5 lakh.
The ICT Division issued the relevant policy on November 11, followed by a formal gazette notification on November 12.
The policy states that these grants will be awarded to transform innovative ideas from early-stage startups into marketable products and services, create new ventures, generate employment, enhance export capabilities, and attract domestic and foreign investment.
Another objective is to ensure transparency, competition, accountability, and result-based financing in government grant management.

item.title: BBS to alter GDP base year
item.description:
The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) has taken the initiative to change the base year for calculating the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to make national economic figures more reliable and up-to-date.
Currently, GDP is calculated using FY15 as the base year.
Under the new initiative, GDP estimates will be rebased using the 2025–26 fiscal year as the new benchmark.
Preliminary survey activities for this transition have already begun.
Alongside this, a specialized expert committee has prepared a draft report on a forensic audit of GDP data.
Necessary administrative actions are being taken based on the observations and recommendations outlined in the report.
These updates were shared today, Wednesday, during the first meeting of the National Statistical Advisory Council (NSAC) for FY27.
Held at the NEC Conference Room in the capital’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, the meeting was chaired by Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury.
The meeting noted that the base year change was initiated to ensure reliable and updated data for national account projections. Surveys conducted for the new base year will make it easier to assess the true size and contribution of various economic sectors.
Meanwhile, steps have been taken to amend the Statistics Act, 2013 to align the country's statistical system with international standards.
Based on recommendations from an expert committee, a final amendment proposal is being drafted.
It includes provisions to incorporate the national statistical system, administrative data, big data, and the United Nations' Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics.
Progress on formulating the National Strategy for the Development of Statistics (NSDS) 2026–30 was also highlighted at the meeting.
Work is underway to finalize the draft strategy in alignment with the government’s five-year reform and development framework, election manifesto, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
Initiatives have also been launched to expand the use of digital technology in data collection.
In BBS field surveys, data is being gathered via tablets and computers using the Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing (CAPI) method.
These operations are being monitored live from a Network Operations Center dashboard.
Additionally, a master plan has been finalized to establish an Integrated Statistical Data Warehouse to store data from various censuses and surveys on a centralized platform.
To expand access to data for research and policymaking, a Microdata Analysis Lab has been set up at the BBS, and a draft policy has been formulated to simplify data publication and accessibility.
The meeting also reviewed the activities of a technical committee working on sample sizes and market assessments to improve data accuracy when compiling the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
Joint efforts have also commenced with the Directorate General of Food to monitor rice market prices and verify data.

item.title: NBR's revenue shortfall for Jul-Oct’FY27 exceeds Tk50,000cr
item.description:
The government's income-expenditure calculus is becoming increasingly challenging.
On one hand, reliance on borrowing to meet budgetary expenses is rising, while on the other, the National Board of Revenue (NBR) is lagging behind in revenue collection.
According to preliminary figures from the NBR, a massive deficit has emerged in meeting revenue targets during the first four months of the current fiscal year (July–October) of FY27.
During this period, the target for revenue collection was nearly Tk178,000 crore.
In contrast, actual collections amounted to less than Tk128,000 crore.
Consequently, the revenue shortfall compared to the target has exceeded Tk50,000 crore.
Earlier, in the first three months of FY27 (July–September), the revenue shortfall stood at approximately Tk43,000 crore.
With the deficit expanding further to cross Tk50,000 crore in the subsequent month, fresh concerns have surfaced regarding the achievement of the government's overall revenue targets.
NBR officials attribute the sluggish revenue growth to a lack of anticipated momentum in economic activity, overly ambitious target setting, and certain policy bottlenecks.
However, despite the widening deficit, collections have increased compared to the same period of the previous FY26.
Yet, this growth rate remains below 6%, whereas revenue growth during the first four months of the last fiscal year exceeded 16%.
According to NBR data, among the three primary revenue sectors, Value Added Tax (VAT) collection is in the worst shape.
During the first four months of the current fiscal year, while income tax and import-level duty collections saw a growth of about 14%, VAT collection registered zero growth.
In fact, collections in this sector declined by nearly 6% compared to the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.
Sources indicate that the government set a revenue collection target of Tk604,000 crore in the budget for the current fiscal year—marking an ambitious 45% jump over actual collections from the previous year.
Never before in the country's history has such a massive increase been targeted in a single fiscal year.
In FY26, revenue collection had grown by 12%, while historical averages hover around 15%.
Consequently, experts and stakeholders had questioned the attainability of the current FY27 targets right from the time of budget announcement.

item.title: Pakistan says minister to make rare India visit for regional talks
item.description:
Pakistan will send a minister to India for a regional conference next week, Islamabad said Saturday, the first such visit since the two foes fought a four-day conflict last year.
Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik will represent Pakistan at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue in New Delhi from November 20 to 22, the Pakistani foreign ministry said in a statement.
It will be the first trip to India by a Pakistani federal minister since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended an SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023.
Nuclear-armed India and Pakistan share a deep distrust and have fought multiple wars since gaining independence in 1947, primarily over the Muslim-majority region of Kashmir, which both countries claim.
In May 2025, the countries fought a deadly four-day conflict after armed gunmen killed over two dozen tourists, mostly Hindus, in Kashmir.
New Delhi has accused Islamabad of backing the attack, a charge vehemently denied by Pakistan.
The attack triggered a series of tit-for-tat diplomatic measures, spiralling into intense exchanges of missile, drone and artillery fire and leaving more than 70 people dead.
“The Government of Pakistan remains committed to promoting dialogue among civilizations and fostering people-to-people contacts within the SCO framework in a spirit of mutual respect,” the foreign ministry said.

item.title: Zelensky: US proposes Ukraine cede territory in exchange for joining Nato
item.description:
The United States suggested for the first time that Ukraine cede land to Russia in exchange for joining Nato, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released Saturday, adding that Russia had rejected an energy target ceasefire at talks this week.
Zelensky said Russia was “betting everything” on this winter’s campaign in its war with Ukraine, while warning that the Kremlin’s demands to redraw Europe’s security architecture are “dangerous” and could lead to more wars.
Zelensky spoke to the media Friday after visits to Denmark and Ireland, where he met with European leaders following two days of US-brokered Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi.
The talks ended with no breakthrough in Europe’s worst war since World War II, but all sides agreed that European officials should be included in future negotiations.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said in the comments kept under embargo until Saturday.
He said Ukraine was discussing “specific security guarantees from Nato and the EU” and that if Western countries confirmed them “then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not? I have no right to make that decision on my own.”
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff attended the Abu Dhabi talks and then met after with Putin and Zelensky separately.
Moscow turned down a proposal for a ceasefire in attacks on energy targets at the Abu Dhabi talks, Zelensky said.
“On the proposal for an energy ceasefire: the Russians don’t want it,” Zelensky said.
Putin’s proposal for a “humanitarian mission” to Kostyantynivka, Zelensky said, was a ploy to get Kyiv to withdraw from the embattled city and open the road to more settlements in the Donetsk region.
Russia said this year that it had seized the town but Ukraine has said fighting is ongoing.
“Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city that way,” Zelensky said.
Moscow’s troops have inched westwards since launching the invasion in February 2022, but have been unable to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.
Zelensky said the EU and Nato are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because... it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations.”

item.title: Myanmar airstrike on displaced persons camp kills 12
item.description:
A Myanmar military airstrike on a camp housing people displaced by the civil war killed 12 people in the westernmost state of Rakhine, witnesses and a rescue worker said on Saturday.
Chit Su Wai, a 27-year-old shopkeeper, sobbed as she described how her daughter, aunt and mother were killed on Friday evening in Byar La IDP camp in Ponnagyun township, northeast of state capital Sittwe.
“All I saw was their bodies scattered in pain. I could not find words to describe it. And we were lost with crying,” she said.
“It has broken our family. There were no others except my family. We did not hear the sound of the fighter jet -– it just came and dropped the bombs.”
Myanmar has been consumed by civil war since the military staged a coup five years ago, provoking armed resistance from democracy activists and ethnic minority factions that have long held sway in the nation’s fringes.
The western coastal state of Rakhine is among the regions worst hit by the war. Controlled almost entirely by the ethnic minority Arakan Army (AA), it has been blockaded by the military and pummelled with regular airstrikes.
It was not possible to contact the Myanmar military for comment on the latest attack.
Chit Su Wai said 12 people died in Friday’s attack, a toll confirmed by Khine Hein Htet, chairman of the Phyusin Yin Khwin Foundation, a rescue and emergency service.
Khine Hein Htet said a five-year-old was among the dead, while 18 were also injured in the camp, where many residents had been living for four years.
“They believed the camp was safe, and they sheltered there together. When we arrived at the scene, most of the victims had died in one place,” the 24-year-old said.
He said it was not a combat area, adding: “We never thought this camp would be targeted.”
The village was a mess of collapsed bamboo houses on Saturday, the wreckage of an upturned vehicle mixed among the debris of household goods and clothes.
Locals had already removed the bodies, wrapping them in yellow and red plastic and burying them in makeshift graves.
Aung Kyaw Min, a 45-year-old tuktuk driver, described how he rushed to the village where his brother and sister lived after hearing of the attack.
“My sister’s body was already headless while my brother was lying dead,” he said, crying.
The next day, he discovered his mother had also been killed, while other relatives, including a 10-year-old, were missing.
His sister was a seamstress who took care of their mother. His brother was a tuktuk driver like him.
“Now all of them -- my sister, brother, including my mother -- were all killed. My niece and nephews are still missing, I don’t know where to find them,” he said.
The Acled monitor estimates that more than 100,000 people have been killed in Myanmar on all sides since the civil war began.

item.title: Tk5cr per MP: LGD’s proposal sparks questions over source and accountability
item.description:
The Local Government Division has sought a special development allocation of Tk5 crore for each member of parliament (MP), Tk1,500 crore in all for 300 MPs, to meet what it calls the urgent needs of people in their constituencies.
But the money is proposed to come not from a new source, but from the annual development funds of upazila parishads and city corporations, raising questions over the impact on local government’s own development activities and the role of MPs in grassroots decisions.
With allegations of irregularities, nepotism and politicisation having surfaced over earlier allocations to MPs, the debate now centres less on whether the money is needed than on where it comes from, who will control its spending, and who will be held accountable.
According to Local Government Ministry sources, Local Government Division Senior Secretary Md Shahidul Hassan sent two separate letters to Finance Division Secretary Dr Md Khairuzzaman Mazumder on November 10.
The proposal seeks Tk1,320 crore for 264 MPs outside city corporation areas, at Tk5 crore each, and Tk180 crore for 36 MPs in city corporation areas, bringing the total to Tk1,500 crore.
The letters state that the money will be spent on renovating educational and religious institutions, providing assistance to poor and meritorious students, the welfare of helpless people, and sports and cultural activities.
The local government secretary noted in the letter that people’s expectations have increased following the restoration of the democratic system after long-standing deprivation and discrimination. MPs hear about people’s small but urgent problems when visiting their constituencies, he wrote, but these needs cannot be met with the limited allocations available under the existing discretionary fund.
A senior Local Government Division official confirmed to Dhaka Tribune that the letters have been sent to the Finance Ministry. Speaking on condition of anonymity, he said the allocation currently available to MPs in the discretionary fund is very insignificant, and questioned how much of a constituency’s needs can be met with only Tk5 lakh.
He said the letters were sent with the consent of MPs from both the ruling and opposition parties, and that opposition MPs will receive the same amount as ruling party MPs.
“During the Awami League’s tenure, there were instances of special development allocations of Tk15 crore and later Tk20 crore for MPs. Compared to that, this is much less. Besides, all MPs will use this money in the interest of developing their respective areas,” he said.
However, alongside the argument for equal allocations, questions have arisen over how justified it is to give the same amount to all constituencies when population, poverty, infrastructure gaps and actual needs vary.
Special development allocations for MPs are not new. Allocations of Tk15 crore and Tk20 crore per MP were made in the past under constituency-based rural infrastructure development projects. The current government also has an initiative to undertake separate projects worth Tk50 crore per MP over five years through the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED), covering roads, bridges and other infrastructure prioritised by MPs. Development researchers have therefore questioned how the new Tk5 crore proposal will be coordinated with earlier initiatives.
In a 2020 study, Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) reviewed 628 development works in 50 parliamentary constituencies. It found instances of low-quality work, unethical transactions between contractors and those concerned, and political influence, along with a lack of transparency and supervision from planning to implementation.
TIB Executive Director Dr Iftekharuzzaman said analysis of past experience and data showed that the bulk of block allocations was used for politicisation in the name of development, creating opportunities for widespread irregularities, corruption, embezzlement and wastage of public money. “The expectation from the current government is that it will move away from this past practice,” he said.
Experts have also raised concerns about the source of the money, which is proposed to come from the annual development funds of upazila parishads and city corporations. They fear this may curtail local governments’ own priority-based development activities.
Articles 59 and 60 of the Constitution establish the basis for the responsibilities and powers of local government institutions, while the primary constitutional responsibilities of MPs are to enact laws and ensure government accountability. Existing laws, however, give MPs an advisory role in local development.
The Local Government Division’s budget for the current 2026-27 fiscal year is Tk40,246 crore, approximately 9% lower than the previous fiscal year’s revised allocation. Amid this, demands have been raised to assess the impact of reallocating funds from existing development funds.
Political analyst Ruhin Hossain Prince told Dhaka Tribune: “First, in my view, the development allocations provided for MPs and ministers for local development are not supported by our Constitution. In other words, this is contradictory to the Constitution. Second, what we say about strengthening local government is also affected. Third, such allocations create opportunities for MPs to assume the role of landlords.”
“Since we are trying to move towards democracy, local government must be strengthened. If public participation and accountability cannot be ensured, the benefits of democracy will not reach the actual people. Considering that, it is necessary to stay away from this kind of allocation and keep MPs away from it as well. This money should be spent through local government while ensuring complete transparency,” he added.
Those concerned say that if the allocation is approved, it must be made clear who will be responsible for selecting projects or beneficiaries, releasing funds, implementation and auditing. In particular, a policy is needed on whether the money will be spent on MPs’ recommendations or whether MPs will be able to make spending decisions directly.
They warn that unless spending information is made public, local participation is ensured, independent audits are conducted and effective action is taken against irregularities, the special allocations risk becoming a tool for political influence.
With the proposal justified by the need to meet people’s urgent needs, how the source of the funds and control over their spending will be determined is now the key question.

item.title: BGB: Tk273.37 crore smuggled goods, drugs seized in October
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) seized smuggled goods, arms, and narcotics worth Tk273.37 crore across the country, including border areas, during nationwide drives in October.
The seized goods include 1.435kg of gold, 13,778 sarees, 2,168,500 liters of edible oil, 381 mobile phones, 2,85,034 healthcare items, vehicle parts, timber, coal, and 207 vehicles and boats used in trafficking.
BGB personnel also recovered weapons, including one SMG, six pistols, five other arms, seven magazines, 120 rounds of ammunition, and 19 cocktails, BGB said in a press release on Saturday.
During the month, huge quantities of narcotics were seized, including 40,45,412 Yaba tablets, 8.097kg of crystal meth (ice), 941 grams of heroin, 1,201 bottles of Phensedyl, 11,307 bottles of foreign liquor, and 1,564kg of hemp.
Besides, 219 smugglers were arrested, while legal action was taken against 114 Bangladeshis, seven Indians, and 350 Myanmar nationals for illegal border crossing.

item.title: Bangladesh to withdraw from global treaty on shipbreaking waste management
item.description:
In 1986, a ship named Pelican, loaded with fly ash, set sail from the port of Philadelphia in the United States. The ship drifted in the sea for two years.

No country allowed it to anchor because it carried 14,000 tonnes of polluted ash harmful to the environment and human health.

On a morning in October 1988, the captain of the ship announced that they had dumped the ash off the coast of a country, but he did not mention the name of the country. It was later revealed that the country was Haiti.

This led to a storm of protests worldwide. The detailed account of this incident is documented in a report titled "Planet of the Year: A Sinking Mess" on the 2 January 1989 issue of the world-renowned Time Magazine.

Facing global protests, on 22 March 1989, the United Nations initiated the ‘Basel Convention’ to regulate waste movement from one country to another. Its full name is ‘The Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal. ’ A total of 170 countries, including Bangladesh, have signed the convention.

However, at the request of shipbreaking industry owners, the Bangladesh government has decided to withdraw from the Basel Convention’s section on shipbreaking.

In August, the cabinet formed a committee to review the laws, rules, policies, and related aspects of the shipbreaking industry, with Environment, Forest, and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo as the head.

On 29 September, this committee decided to exit the Basel Convention and follow the Hong Kong Convention in the matter of shipbreaking.

It is noteworthy that the Basel Convention establishes control over international waste movement. On the other hand, the Hong Kong Convention primarily deals with safe shipbreaking-related issues in yards.

Mohammad Mohsin, the president of the Bangladesh Ship Breakers and Ship Recyclers Association, told Prothom Alo that efforts are being made to make the shipbreaking industry safe by following the Hong Kong Convention. For this, each yard is required to invest Tk 1.5 billion to 2 billion.

Mohammad Mohsin stated, “Hong Kong Convention and Basel Convention are like two different physicians for the same disease. We want any one of them to cure this disease. In this case, we have requested the government to follow the Hong Kong Convention because the International Labour Organisation (ILO), the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), and those who manage shipping lines are all linked with the Hong Kong Convention.”

However, environmental experts say that the Hong Kong Convention does not consider ships as waste. Therefore, shipbreaking industry owners prefer the Hong Kong Convention.

Syeda Rizwana Hasan, the chief executive of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA), told Prothom Alo that the shipbreaking industry is a tactic to smuggle developed countries' waste under the guise of shipbreaking; which can be proven through the Basel Convention. That’s why shipbreaking industry owners do not want to remain under the Basel Convention.

What’s in the Basel Convention

According to Article 2 of the Basel Convention, expired ships are considered hazardous waste. For example, a ship suitable for sea travel but its owner decides not to use it for commercial transport and wants to sell it to a yard in Bangladesh for breaking. In such a situation, the ship would be considered waste under the Basel Convention.

The Basel Convention does not ban the import or scrapping of all expired ships; rather, it imposes control over transboundary movements of ships defined as waste and those carrying hazardous waste.

According to Article 6 of the Basel Convention, before exporting hazardous waste, the exporting country must inform the importing country about the waste. It would then have to obtain written consent from the importing country. An agreement between the exporting and importing countries must exist for the environmentally sound disposal of waste.

Article 8 states that if the waste cannot be disposed of according to the agreement, the exporting country must take back the waste.

Environment, Forest, and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo told Prothom Alo, “Everything relating to shipbreaking is overseen by the IMO. The Hong Kong Convention is under the IMO. Our green yards are also constructed in light of the Hong Kong Convention.”

Assuring that there will be no problems with waste management, the minister mentioned that each green yard has specialised places for storing waste. Some waste is sold to vendors licensed by the Department of Environment. In addition, a TSDF (Treatment, Storage, and Disposal Facility) for shipbreaking waste management is being constructed in Mirsarai.

What international experts are saying

The Brussels-based international organisation ‘NGO Shipbreaking Platform’ has been working for a long time to ensure a safe working environment for workers in the shipbreaking industry.

In response to written questions from Prothom Alo, Ingvild Jenssen, the founder and executive director of the platform, stated that Bangladesh needs to adhere to the Basel Convention. This global convention is crucial to stopping the dumping of toxic waste and protecting the environment and human health from the harm of hazardous substances.

She mentioned that if Bangladesh moves away from the Basel Convention concerning abandoned ships, the marine ecosystem and coastal environment will be at greater risk, and coastal residents will be in danger.

Jenssen advised that both the Basel and Hong Kong Conventions could be effectively implemented alongside each other; rather, if both conventions are enforced together, the protection of the environment and workers would be stronger. She pointed out that the regulations for safe and environmentally sound shipbreaking in the Hong Kong Convention are weak.

Why the Hong Kong Convention is weak

The Basel Convention was established under the initiative of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), whereas the Hong Kong Convention falls under the United Nations Maritime Organization (IMO).
The International Chamber of Shipping and European Shipowners conducted an independent study last June through the Netherlands-based research organisation CE Delft.

This study, titled ‘Assessing Global Standard For Ship Recycling, ’ identified three major weaknesses of the Hong Kong Convention. These are the approval and inspection of shipbreaking yards, subsequent management of hazardous waste, and the scope of the list of hazardous materials.

The study states that the convention does not ban open beach shipbreaking methods in Bangladesh, India, and Pakistan. There is a risk that oil, heavy metals, and toxic waste may mix with soil and water due to shipbreaking on beaches.

According to the Hong Kong Convention, the responsibility for managing hazardous waste primarily falls on the importing countries. Ship owners or the source countries of waste are not held accountable for the waste. However, under the Basel Convention, the exporting country must inform the importing country before sending waste and obtain a letter of consent.

item.title: US suggested Kyiv cede land to Russia in exchange for joining NATO, Zelensky says
item.description:
UKRAINE-CRISIS/ZELENSKIY-TALKS

Washington has suggested Ukraine cede land to Russia in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in comments released Saturday, adding that it indicated his country's ties with the Western military alliance are "back on the agenda".

Zelensky also warned the Kremlin was "betting everything" on this winter's military campaign.

Moscow has pounded Ukraine in the run-up to the colder months, with Russian President Vladimir Putin showing no sign of backing down.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met both Putin and Zelensky separately on Thursday after two days of talks with their delegations in Abu Dhabi, which ended with no breakthrough.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said.

US approves $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine

"After providing Ukraine with this kind of defence support, seeing this kind of development of our army and this strength in our defence, they cannot simply let Ukraine go," he added.

He said the discussion showed that "NATO is back on the agenda" for Ukraine.

Ukraine has long sought to enter the military alliance, which Moscow has considered a red line.

NATO and Washington have not yet commented directly on Zelensky's account.

Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, later posted on X that media had reported "maximalist propositions proposed by both sides, along with strong political rhetoric".

"However, we are determined to continue the hard work, maintain the confidentiality necessary for sensitive negotiations, and find a pathway to end this horrible war," he said, adding "several new ideas emerged from the discussions and are now being explored."

This week's meetings have led to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war.

In Dublin on Friday, Europe chose five countries -- France, Germany, Italy, the UK and Poland -- to send representatives to the talks.

Russia meanwhile continued its bombardment of Ukraine on Saturday, with deadly strikes in the eastern city of Pavlohrad and in a village near Zaporizhzhia, which is now just a few dozen kilometres from the front line.

Kyiv seeks guarantees

Zelensky said Kyiv was discussing security guarantees with Western partners and that Ukrainians would ultimately decide whether to accept any deal.

He insisted Ukraine would not recognise any land seized by Moscow's troops as Russian.

Russia has consistently said Kyiv joining NATO is a red line and in 2022 launched its invasion saying the West planned to incorporate Ukraine into the alliance.

Trump's administration has for almost two years tried to reach a breakthrough in talks between Russia and Ukraine.

The Kremlin has also ruled out foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine and wider ceasefires.

But Putin earlier this week proposed a "humanitarian" mission to the eastern town of Kostyantynivka, which Moscow announced it had seized in the summer but where Kyiv says fighting continues.

Zelensky said the proposal was a bid to advance Russian gains in Donetsk. "Their next steps will be our other cities in Donbas," he said.

Russian troops have inched westwards but have been unable to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.

'First, end the war'

Russia has tried to reframe negotiations on ending the war -- Europe's worst since World War II -- into a conversation on the continent's wider security.

In 2021, before its Ukraine invasion, Moscow issued an ultimatum to the West to pull back NATO troops from eastern Europe.

Moscow's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, this week called for a "new, modern Yalta", drawing criticism from European leaders.

Zelensky warned that any discussion of wider security arrangements should come only after the war has ended.

European leaders have reacted coolly to the proposal for a new security architecture.

"We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," Germany's Friedrich Merz said Friday.

French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that "those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it" and, by extension, all of Europe.

"That is the spirit of defeat. That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France's position," Macron said.

"Helping Ukraine defend itself is protecting France and the French," he added.
