Climate adaptation funding shortfall puts Bangladesh under pressure
item.description:
Even after 17 years of Cyclone Aila, the homestead of Md Zia Gain and his wife, Shamima Begum, in Mothbari village of Koyra upazila, Khulna, remains submerged beneath the waters of the Shakbaria River.

A nearly three-kilometre-long and 250-metre-wide channel, formed by tidal currents after an embankment collapsed, has swallowed their home. They now live on the slope of the embankment of the river.

The house of Minoti Sana, a woman in her 60's from the same village, also once stood in what is now the middle of the river. Her land has remained unrecovered since Cyclone Aila.

Ismail Gazi, Yunus Ali and Ilias Gazi, along with many other villagers, share similar stories. They lost their homesteads and have been living on the slopes of embankments for the past 17 years.

Natural disasters are nothing new in Bangladesh. However, the loss of homes, rising salinity and shortages of safe drinking water in coastal areas continue to transform people's lives over the long term. How to address these challenges is being discussed at the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye.

The United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP) Adaptation Gap Report 2026, published ahead of the conference, highlights the shortfall in climate adaptation finance.

How much funding is needed for adaptation?

According to Bangladesh's third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), the country needs US$8.5 billion annually to implement its adaptation priorities. The same document estimates that the average annual flow of funding for adaptation in the country stands at around US$4 billion.

This leaves an annual shortfall of US$4.5 billion, equivalent to approximately Tk 561.38 billion (Tk 56,138 crore), at an exchange rate of Tk 124.75 per US dollar.

NDC 3.0 states that Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing requirements could rise to between US$12 billion and US$14 billion by 2035.

At the same exchange rate, this would amount to approximately Tk 1,497 billion to Tk 1,746.5 billion (Tk 149,700 crore to Tk 174,650 crore).

Growing needs, insufficient funding

Bangladesh's National Adaptation Plan (NAP) estimates that the country will need a total of US$230 billion to implement 113 initiatives between 2023 and 2050. This amounts to an average of approximately US$8.5 billion annually over 27 years.

The initiatives cover various sectors, including water, agriculture, fisheries and livestock, urban development, disaster management, biodiversity and institutional capacity-building.

UNEP's report draws its estimate of Bangladesh's annual adaptation financing needs of US$12–14 billion by 2035 from the country's third NDC.

The report also states that international public adaptation finance from developed countries to developing nations stood at US$28.7 billion in 2024, an increase of just US$1 billion from the previous year.

The annual adaptation financing needs of developing countries could reach approximately US$305 billion by 2035. This estimate uses 2024 prices and excludes the requirements of the private sector. Including private-sector needs could almost double the total requirement.

At COP30, countries called for adaptation finance to increase at least threefold by 2035. According to UNEP's estimates, even if this target is achieved, it would meet only 20 to 29 per cent of the potential adaptation financing needs of developing countries.

The nature of the financing also matters. In 2024, loans accounted for 55 per cent of international public adaptation finance for developing countries, while grants made up 44 per cent. Nearly half of the loans came on market-based or non-concessional terms.

Experts say Bangladesh needs more grants and low-interest, long-term financing to meet its adaptation costs without placing further pressure on public debt.

Climate finance expert Haseeb Muhammad Irfanullah told Prothom Alo, "Reports published ahead of the COP conferences help us understand changes in the nature and flow of adaptation finance and provide useful insights for negotiations. However, a significant funding gap remains in the flow of finance from developed to developing countries."

Bangladesh still bears the cost of climate damage

According to UNEP's report, Bangladesh allocated at least US$400 million from its revenue budget to the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund between 2010 and the 2017–18 fiscal year. During this period, the authorities approved 512 projects across 18 ministries.

At least 45 per cent of the fund, or more than US$180 million, went towards adaptation activities. However, this amount remains inadequate compared with the country's potential annual requirement of US$12–14 billion.

The Climate Budget Report for the 2026–27 fiscal year estimates climate-related expenditure of Tk 517.46 billion (Tk 51,746 crore) across 25 ministries and divisions. Of this amount, Tk 389.06 billion (Tk 38,906 crore) is allocated to adaptation.

The national budget also proposes an allocation of Tk 1 billion (Tk 100 crore) for the Bangladesh Climate Change Trust Fund.

However, the overall figure for climate-related expenditure does not represent a separate allocation for new adaptation projects. Rather, it reflects climate-related spending identified within the budgets of various ministries and divisions.

Adaptation can reduce climate risks, but it cannot prevent all losses and damage. In the first funding round of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, 119 developing countries applied for US$2.8 billion.

However, the fund initially had only US$342 million, equivalent to around one-eighth of the total demand. Complex application procedures and limited institutional capacity also pose barriers to accessing support.

Farah Anjum, Bangladesh country lead at the Global Strategic Communications Council, who is attending COP31, told Prothom Alo, "Although Bangladesh faces significant climate risks, its contribution to global emissions is low. Yet the country has to bear much of the substantial cost of adaptation from its own resources. Developed countries should go beyond their existing commitments and provide accessible grant-based financing, technology transfer and technical assistance. They must also ensure that allocated funds reach vulnerable communities and effectively reduce climate-related losses and damage."

item.title: 294 murders a month on average as 2,938 murder cases filed in 10 months
item.description:
Sheikh Zakir Hossain, a leader of ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), was shot dead inside his shop at Rupsa upazila in Khulna on Thursday night. Over the past 22 days, six people have been killed and another six injured in shootings in Khulna. 

Such killings are not confined to Khulna alone; rather, they are taking place across the country. A total of 2,938 murder cases were filed nationwide in the first 10 months of this year, averaging nearly 294 a month.

Alongside murders, incidents of extortion, robbery, mugging and the public use of firearms have heightened concerns over law and order in the country. 

People from various walks of life say the law-and-order situation has yet to improve as expected, even eight months after the government took office. The police, however, say law and order collapsed following the mass uprising but the situation has been gradually improving.

Analysing the killings and related data, officials involved in investigations say most murders stemmed from political violence, extortion, attempts to establish dominance, youth gangs and disputes over control of the drug trade. Many others were the result of domestic violence.

An analysis of case records from the police headquarters shows that 170,101 cases involving various crimes were filed across the country between January and October this year. A total of 181,673 cases were filed in the whole of the previous year. Besides murder cases, 417 robbery cases, 1,519 cases of banditry and 867 kidnapping cases were filed in the first 10 months of this year.

According to police headquarters data, 218 murder cases were filed in Dhaka over the past 10 months, the highest figure among the eight metropolitan police areas. Most recently, 19 murder cases were filed in October, compared with 31 in September. 

A single case is sometimes filed over multiple incidents. Therefore, the number of cases does not necessarily reflect the actual number of crimes committed.

An analysis of case records from the eight metropolitan police units and nine police ranges shows that Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) recorded the highest number of murder cases among the metropolitan areas, with 218 in the past 10 months. Among the nine ranges, Dhaka Range recorded the highest number, with 673 murder cases, followed by Chattogram Range with 571.

Kamarum Munira, spokesperson for police headquarters and an assistant inspector general (AIG), told Prothom Alo that the police were taking a range of measures to prevent murders and bring perpetrators to justice. 

These included identifying crime-prone areas, keeping criminals under intelligence surveillance, recovering illegal firearms, arresting criminals and goons, and conducting regular raids, she added.

The police headquarters spokesperson further said instructions had been issued to promptly register cases involving every murder, collect forensic evidence and identify perpetrators through investigations.

Kamarum Munira added that the recent killings in Khulna were being treated as a matter of particular concern. A decision had been taken to conduct special joint operations involving law enforcement agencies to curb crime and extortion there. Other initiatives included strengthening checkpoints, patrols and intelligence surveillance on major roads, as well as launching drives against unregistered motorcycles.

218 murders in Dhaka

In April, top criminal Khandaker Naim Ahmed Titon was shot dead in broad daylight in the capital's New Market area. On 9 November, a young woman named Sanjida Akter Ima, 22, was strangled to death at a house in Uttarkhan, Dhaka.

According to police headquarters data, 218 murder cases were filed in Dhaka over the past 10 months, the highest figure among the eight metropolitan police areas. Most recently, 19 murder cases were filed in October, compared with 31 in September. 

The murders of four members of the same family in Rangpur, five members of a family in Kapasia, Gazipur, and a mother and her three daughters in Lakshmipur also drew nationwide attention.

DMP officials say between 20 and 30 murders take place every month across the jurisdiction of its 50 police stations.

Notable murders outside Dhaka

Several high-profile murders have taken place in different parts of the country over the past 10 months. Most recently, BNP leader and brick-and-sand trader Mohammad Zakir Hossain was shot dead inside a shop in the village of Sholpo Bahirdia in Rupsa, Khulna, on Thursday night.

Speaking at his funeral prayers (namaz-e-ianaza), Nazrul Islam Manju, administrator of Khulna City Corporation and a BNP leader, said Khulna had become engulfed in crimes, with murders, extortion and drug trading rampant. 

People were being killed for speaking out against these activities, he said. He called for joint operations to arrest listed criminals.

Between 22 October and 12 November, at least 13 shooting incidents took place in Khulna over 22 days. In one incident, criminals fired blank shots at a clinic after demanding extortion money. Six people were killed and another six injured in the shootings. Three more people were killed in attacks involving sharp weapons and beatings. 

In all, nine people were murdered in Khulna during the 22-day period: five in Khulna city, three in Rupsa and one in Dumuria upazilas. Up to 12 November this year, 39 murders had been recorded in Khulna city and 40 across the district.

Earlier, on 18 September, Ishayat Shahriar, also known as Apratim, 13, son of Nahida Begum, an associate professor in the Department of Bangla at Comilla University, was killed by members of a youth gang. The incident sparked widespread discussion across the country.

At around 8:30 pm on 15 October, journalist Lutfozzaman Alif Fakir, 44, was shot dead in Netrokona. Alif had reported on smuggling, drug and arms trafficking along the border, as well as local irregularities and wrongdoing. He regularly published photographs and videos exposing these activities. There are allegations that he was targeted and killed for his reporting.

The murders of four members of the same family in Rangpur, five members of a family in Kapasia, Gazipur, and a mother and her three daughters in Lakshmipur also drew nationwide attention.

item.title: More than half of Bangladesh’s births are now C-sections
item.description:
More than half of the babies born in Bangladesh now arrive through caesarean section.
But how many of those operations are truly necessary?
According to the Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNICEF, 51.8% of deliveries in the country now take place through the caesarean method, nearly three times the rate of 12 years ago. The World Health Organization (WHO) says caesarean sections should not be performed without medical necessity, and that a rate of 10% to 15% at the population level is the most appropriate.
The question has become a point of sharp disagreement. Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain says the trend of unnecessary operations has increased at an alarming rate, and alleges that some private clinics and broker networks frighten families into them.
Doctors say they try for normal delivery, that a caesarean is sometimes medically essential, and that some mothers themselves ask for one.
Experts say each pregnancy must be judged on its own circumstances, and that ensuring hospitals are accountable is now a major challenge.
Two days before the last Eid-ul-Azha, at around 7:45am, Fahmid Ahmed (pseudonym) was admitted to a private hospital in the capital with his pregnant wife. Throughout the pregnancy they had been under the care of a doctor at that hospital. Both the mother and the unborn child were in good physical condition, and the couple were mentally prepared for childbirth through the normal process.
Immediately after admission, they were asked, “Have you come for an operation?” The couple were surprised and said they had come for a normal delivery.
A new experience then began. Every now and then, the hospital’s assistant doctors would come to the pregnant mother and say, “Normal delivery is very painful”, “It is very difficult”, and “There will be a lot of complications”. At one point her husband protested: “Why are you saying such things? Where you should be giving encouragement, you are doing the opposite by frightening her.”
As the necessary medical tests continued, the assistant doctors said the unborn child had moved towards the upper part of the abdomen and would have to be delivered through an operation.
The couple still did not give up hope. They contacted the doctor who had treated them throughout the pregnancy and discussed the matter, but that brought no solution. Finally, at around 10:30pm, the woman gave birth through an operation.
From the beginning, the doctor had said he would make every possible effort for a normal delivery. The couple’s experience was different.
Their experience is one part of the overall picture of childbirth among women in the country. Every day, many women like her have to give birth through operations.
The caesarean rate in the country was 19.1% in 2012-13. In 2019, it increased to 36%. In 2025, it reached 51.8%.
The rate varies according to urban and rural areas and economic status. It is 56% in urban areas and 50% in rural areas. Among women from the wealthiest families, 68% give birth through caesarean sections. The rate is 57% in the fourth wealthiest group, 52% in the middle group and 34% among the poorest families.
According to the WHO, caesarean sections should not be performed without medical necessity. Although caesarean rates are increasing worldwide, this has not increased health benefits; rather, the risks for mothers and children have increased. The organisation says a caesarean rate of 10% to 15% at the population level is the most appropriate.
Dr Kishwar Sultana, professor of the Department of Gynaecology and Obstetrics at Holy Family Red Crescent Medical College and Hospital, told Dhaka Tribune there are multiple reasons behind the increase.
First, she said, it needs to be examined whether the rate is increasing more in the private or public sector. Some private-sector hospitals are still not being brought fully under monitoring, and some centres are operated for commercial purposes. However, this cannot be said about all institutions. In some cases, there may be a lack of proper supervision.
Another reason is that mothers who previously had a caesarean section also have to undergo caesarean sections for subsequent childbirths. Some mothers also think that they will have two children, so there is no need to go through the pain of normal delivery. This is called maternal choice.
Pointing out that some matters on the doctors’ side also need to be considered, she said the safety of mother and child is important to doctors. There is no guarantee that both will be fine simply because a normal delivery takes place, and the lengthy process of normal delivery also needs to be considered. Even then, doctors try for normal delivery, but many times patients’ families do not want to accept this. Whenever any problem occurs, the blame is placed on the doctor. No doctor wants anything bad to happen to their patient. However, there is no scope to deny that medical negligence has occurred in some cases, but it is also not right to hold all doctors responsible.
She said repeat caesarean sections are also a major reason. If a mother has a caesarean section once, a caesarean is also performed for her subsequent childbirth. Even for the delivery of a third or fourth child, a caesarean has to be performed. If someone has had two caesarean sections before and is pregnant again, it is assumed that she will have to undergo a caesarean for the third time as well. This is how the number is increasing.
Professor Sultana said that if a woman comes to a doctor and wants a normal delivery, it is her right. If everything is fine during pregnancy, she is advised accordingly, and they wait until the scheduled date. If labour pains do not begin even after that, it is possible to wait and observe for another two to four days, or even up to seven days, while the baby’s heartbeat is monitored.
However, caution is needed from the beginning in some pregnancies. If the mother’s blood pressure rises significantly, the condition of the unborn child deteriorates, the baby’s heartbeat becomes abnormal or the baby passes stool inside the womb, delivery has to be performed on an emergency basis. If the mother starts bleeding, quick measures also need to be taken. caesarean sections have to be performed in these cases. Hospitals with maternity services generally have arrangements for emergency caesarean sections 24 hours a day.
Professor Farhana Dewan, former president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh (OGSB), also told Dhaka Tribune that doctors try for normal delivery. It is not that caesarean sections are performed intentionally, she said, and many times patients also want them. However, there are many reasons why caesarean deliveries are more common than normal deliveries.
She said caesarean sections are sometimes necessary for medical reasons, for example if there has been a previous caesarean section, if the baby’s position is not correct, if the amniotic fluid decreases, if the baby’s movements decrease or if the mother has a tumour in her uterus. In such cases, a caesarean is performed through prior planning, which is called an elective caesarean. Even after labour pains begin, an emergency caesarean may be necessary for various reasons. These are the indications for caesarean sections, or medical reasons. If everything is normal, doctors try for normal delivery.
Decisions are sometimes taken considering the safety of the baby as well, she said. Doctors become concerned if the baby cannot be monitored properly or if there is a risk that the baby’s condition may deteriorate. Sometimes, if a caesarean is performed late, the baby may develop breathing difficulties, and there may even be a risk of death.
In an ideal situation, Professor Dewan said, every hospital should have a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), making it possible to provide medical support to newborns when necessary. However, the number of NICU facilities in the country is inadequate compared to the number of deliveries. Many people are unable to receive this service because they do not have the financial means, and beds are often unavailable in government hospitals as well.
In some risky situations, she said, the decision to perform a caesarean is made through prior planning. In other cases, an emergency caesarean has to be performed. For example, if a patient starts bleeding, it is an immediate emergency. Such caesarean sections cannot be performed just anywhere; they have to be performed at a multidisciplinary centre where the necessary facilities and various specialist doctors are available.
Another issue being seen more frequently is maternal request, meaning the mother herself wants a caesarean section. She directly says she will not be able to tolerate the pain of normal delivery and therefore wants a caesarean. This is not seen only in Bangladesh; it is also observed in different countries around the world.
Professor Dewan said mothers are kept under observation throughout pregnancy to determine whether they are prepared for normal delivery. Through regular check-ups, as the scheduled delivery date approaches, it is examined whether the mother has diabetes, high blood pressure or any other physical problem and whether the baby’s position is correct. If everything is fine, normal delivery can be attempted. However, if the mother’s age is very high or she has any other physical problem, additional caution needs to be taken when making the decision.
Professor Dewan said that even if the first child is born through a caesarean section, the second can be delivered through normal delivery. It is necessary, however, to know why the first child was not delivered through normal delivery and why a caesarean had to be performed. Doctors ask every patient about this. If there were reasons such as prolonged labour pains or the cervix not opening even after the scheduled date had passed, normal delivery can be attempted for the second child.
If the mother’s pelvis, or the passage through which the baby is born, is small, there is no possibility of normal delivery. Along with hearing the patient’s previous history, doctors try to understand why a caesarean was performed the first time by examining previous medical documents. If there is a recurring reason that will require a caesarean for subsequent childbirth as well, then it has to be performed. But if a caesarean had to be performed for a temporary reason, such as the baby’s heartbeat decreasing, the water breaking or the umbilical cord coming out first, normal delivery can be attempted for the second child.
At a workshop organised by the Bangladesh Midwifery Society (BMS) on July 6, Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain emphasised the importance of reducing the trend of unnecessary caesarean operations. He said delivery rooms must be established compulsorily at all private clinics and hospitals by July 11, otherwise the licences of the concerned institutions would be cancelled.
The minister said the trend had increased at an alarming rate. At present, he said, a section of people in the country has become excessively profit-oriented, with their main goal being to earn money rather than the welfare of people or the interests of the country. This has also had a negative impact on the healthcare sector.
He said that at one time, most children in the country were born through normal delivery, and there was a long tradition of safe childbirth in rural areas with the assistance of experienced traditional birth attendants. Although healthcare has improved now, the trend of unnecessary caesarean sections for commercial purposes has increased.
Initially, after regular medical examinations, in many cases broker networks and some medical centres frighten family members by warning them of various complications. They create fears such as, “If an operation is not performed, the mother or the child will not survive”, and force families to make the decision to undergo a caesarean section. Naturally, families fall into this trap because they do not want to take risks with the lives of the mother and child.
The minister also alleged that some private clinics and broker networks were encouraging pregnant women to undergo caesarean sections by frightening and intimidating them. He said the government would take strict measures to protect the nation from this situation. At the same time, 100,000 new personnel would be recruited in the health sector, of whom 80,000 would be women, most of them midwifery workers.
Overall, medical necessity, maternal choice, repeat caesarean sections, commercial tendencies among hospitals and limitations in healthcare facilities have emerged as factors behind the increase in the caesarean rate. According to experts, decisions must be made by considering the circumstances of each pregnancy. Creating opportunities for normal delivery by avoiding caesarean sections without medical necessity, and ensuring accountability among hospitals in this regard, are now major challenges.

item.title: Wahid-Uz-Zaman appointed new BTRC chairman
item.description:
Major General (retd) Md Wahid-Uz-Zaman has been appointed chairman of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) for one year on a contractual basis, replacing Major General Md Emdad Ul Bari.
The remaining tenure of Emdad Ul Bari's contractual appointment as BTRC chairman has been cancelled.
The Ministry of Public Administration issued two separate notifications in this regard on Sunday.
According to the notification on the new appointment, Wahid-Uz-Zaman has been appointed under Section 49 of the Government Service Act, 2018, subject to the suspension of his post-retirement leave and related benefits and relinquishment of any other professional or business engagement, as well as employment with any government, semi-government or private institution or organization.
He has been appointed on a contractual basis as commissioner (management and administration) of the BTRC and posted as its chairman for one year from the date of his joining.
Other terms and conditions of the appointment will be determined through a contract, the notification said.

item.title: BB to lift tenure limits on expatriate bonds to boost reserves
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has taken initiatives to collect foreign currency through Non-Resident Convertible (NRC) accounts and relax investment limits and tenure restrictions on three types of bonds introduced for expatriates to boost foreign exchange reserves.
At the same time, the central bank aims to set targets to reduce banks' corporate lending and increase loans in the retail and small and medium enterprise (SME) industries.
There is a plan to bring corporate loans down to 45 percent starting next year.
Bangladesh Bank Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman disclosed these plans Saturday at the "5th Bangladesh Economic Summit-2026," organized by Bonik Barta at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in the capital.
The governor said that NRC accounts have already been launched, and the accounts are being promoted internationally with the assistance of the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
Through similar accounts, India raised $32 billion and Pakistan raised $13 billion within four to five months. Bangladesh also wants to collect foreign currency in this manner.
However, the central bank is also cautious to ensure that repayments under the NRC scheme over the next three to four years do not put major pressure on the reserves.
Noting that the tenure of the three types of bonds currently available to expatriates is capped at a maximum of 15 years, the governor said an initiative has been taken to lift this limit and make the tenure open-ended.
He mentioned that there is currently an investment equivalent to around $604 million to $606 million in these bonds. If the restrictions can be relaxed, more foreign currency will flow into the country, increasing reserves.
Meanwhile, the governor stated that 70% to 80% of private banks' loans are going to the corporate sector.
He said commercial bank licenses were not granted solely for corporate lending, and loan disbursement targets for this sector may be fixed for next year.
He urged bankers to disburse at least 20% of their loans to retail customers and 35% to the SME sector, while bringing the share of corporate loans down to 45%.
The governor added that arrangements must be made for large industrial enterprises to raise their necessary financing from the capital market. This will create purchasing power and demand in the economy and also make it easier for large industrial enterprises to survive.

item.title: Govt cuts import duties on dates, oranges and apples ahead of Ramadan
item.description:
The government on Sunday said import duties on imported dates, oranges, and apples would be reduced temporarily, coinciding with the holy month of Ramadan.
According to an official statement, the cabinet, in its 27th meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman in the chair, decided to reduce duty on imported dates to 5% from 25%, while the rate would remain in effect until March 10, 2027.
It said the import tax on oranges (malta) under HS Code 08051010 and apples under HS Code 08081010 was set at 61%, down from the existing 121.78%, while the makeshift arrangement would remain effective from January 24 to February 23.
The statement said the cabinet gave in-principle and final approval to a revenue board (NBR) proposal to revert from the quarterly setup introduced in the 2026-27 budget, asking standard businesses to submit VAT returns within 15 days of the end of each monthly tax period.
The revised provision is expected to be incorporated in the proposed “Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty (Amendment) Act, 2026” amending an October 2026 ordinance introducing quarterly VAT filing with monthly submissions.
It recalled that the budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year had relaxed the requirement of submitting VAT returns every month, allowing submission within 15 days of the end of every three months in line with the ordinance.
The statement said the change created obstacles for revenue collection at the field level, making it necessary to amend Section 64 of the Value Added Tax and Supplementary Duty Act, 2012.
The amendment is expected to be approved at the current parliament session, subject to Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division vetting.

item.title: Govt plans 108km barbed-wire fencing along Myanmar border
item.description:
The government has taken an initiative to construct and modernise barbed-wire fencing along 108 kilometres of the Bangladesh-Myanmar border as part of its efforts to prevent drug trafficking, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Sunday.
He made the remarks at the sixth meeting of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Home Affairs at the National Parliament Building.
Committee Chairman Zainul Abedin chaired the meeting.
During the meeting, the chairman stressed the need to identify sources of drug production, supply and trafficking and take legal action to eliminate them. He also recommended investigating the financial networks linked to drug trading and tracing the flow of proceeds from criminal activities.
The home minister said the law and order situation across the country remained under control, adding that law enforcement agencies were committed to preventing sabotage and terrorism.
Parliamentary Whip Rakibul Islam stressed the need to introduce advanced technologies at the borders, similar to those used in developed countries. He also called for more effective use of drone surveillance.
Another parliamentary whip, Mia Nur Uddin Ahmed Apu, said controlling drug use required a social movement, stressing that it was a shared national responsibility rather than the sole responsibility of a ministry or a particular law enforcement agency.
The committee recommended ensuring the necessary financial allocations promptly to combat drug-related crimes.
It also reviewed measures to identify vulnerable border areas and routes used for drug smuggling and stressed coordinated surveillance, drives and preventive measures involving Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), Coast Guard, police and the Department of Narcotics Control.
The meeting was attended by committee members, including Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, Parliamentary Whips Rakibul Islam and Mia Nuruddin Ahmed Apu, Md Kamruzzaman, Md Monowar Hossain and Shirin Sultana.
Senior officials, including the senior secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the inspector general of police, director generals of departments under the ministry and heads of relevant agencies, were also present.

item.title: Commerce minister: Bangladesh's trade deficit stands at $24.17b in 2024-25FY
item.description:
Bangladesh's trade deficit with the rest of the world stood at $24.17 billion in the fiscal year 2024-25, with the deficit with India alone amounting to $7.86 billion, Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir told Parliament on Sunday.
“In the 2024-25 fiscal year, exports amounted to $55.19 billion. In contrast, imports totaled $79.36 billion, resulting in a trade deficit of $24.17 billion,” he said, while replying to a question from treasury bench lawmaker Nilufar Chowdhury Moni (Women Seat-10).
During the 2024-25 fiscal year, goods from Bangladesh were exported to 202 destinations, the minister said.
He said the readymade garment (RMG) sector accounted for 84% of the country's export earnings.
Replying to a question from opposition Jamaat-e-Islami lawmaker Md Keramat Ali (Chapainawabganj-1), the commerce minister said Bangladesh, as a member of the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) and the Asia-Pacific Trade Agreement (APTA), enjoys duty-free and quota-free access to the Indian market for all products except 25 items, including tobacco and alcoholic beverages.
According to the statistics placed by him, Bangladesh had trade deficits with four Saarc member countries – Afghanistan, Bhutan, India and Pakistan, while positive imbalance with three other Saarc members in favour of Bangladesh.
Among the Saarc countries, Bangladesh had the highest trade deficit with India, which stood at $7,860 million in the fiscal year 2024-25.
Meanwhile, replying to a question from Opposition Chief whip and NCP lawmaker Nahid Islam (Dhaka-11), the minister said Bangladesh's trade deficit with India stood at $9,246.41 million in the fiscal year 2025-26.
During that fiscal year, Bangladesh exported goods worth $1,802.17 million to India against imports worth $11,048.58 million from the country, he said.
Responding to a question from independent lawmaker Sk Mozibur Rahman Iqbal (Kishoreganj-5), Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said Bangladesh earned $13,746.35 million from RMG exports during July-October of the current fiscal year 2026-27.
The earnings marked a 5.82% increase from $12,990.36 million recorded during the same period of the previous fiscal year, he said.
Replying to a question from ruling party lawmaker Md Abul Kalam (Comilla-9), the commerce minister said the Dhaka International Trade Fair 2026 generated export orders worth Tk224.26 crore, which was 42.79% lower than the Tk392 crore recorded at the fair in 2025.
In response to a supplementary question from BNP lawmaker Nadia Pathan Papon (Women Seat-32), the commerce minister expressed optimism that the supply of essential commodities would be better during the upcoming Ramadan than in the previous year.
“Considering the market situation so far, we hope prices will remain within a tolerable range during the next Ramadan, provided there is no natural disaster or major change in the international situation,” he said.

item.title: Law minister assures no repeat of Ziaul Ahsan-like instance on court premises
item.description:
Law Minister Md. Asaduzzaman on Sunday assured the National Parliament that instances such as the one involving former army officer Ziaul Ahsan on court premises will not be repeated.
He also vowed that justice would be ensured for every killing, enforced disappearance, and rights violation committed in the country, including during the July mass uprising.
Replying to a query from Sylhet-2 MP Tahsina Rushdir Luna in Parliament regarding the ‘picnic type’ approach of Ziaul Ahsan while entering and leaving the ICT, the minister spoke about Ziaul Ahsan, former director general of the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC), who is now facing trial at the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) on charges of crimes against humanity.
The minister said the matter had been raised in the House and had come to his attention.
Although what happens when an accused is taken to court does not fall under the law minister's jurisdiction, he said the government took note of the issue once it came to light.
He said the accused was subsequently taken away in the manner required for a "notorious criminal".
"We assure you, honourable speaker, that such incidents will not recur at court premises," he said.
The minister said the government was keen to ensure that justice was not called into question in any way, while at the same time not seeking any "tailor-made" judgment.
Agreeing with the sentiments expressed by the MP, the minister reaffirmed the government's commitment to pursue justice for all unlawful killings, enforced disappearances and other atrocities in Bangladesh's history, as well as for those killed, maimed, blinded or otherwise injured during the July mass uprising.
Referring to a recent statement by the home minister under Rule 300, the law minister said teams led by the chief investigation officer and the chief prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal would visit districts outside Dhaka where crimes against humanity were committed over the past 16 years and during the July uprising.
The teams will investigate enforced disappearances, killings, political persecution and other crimes against humanity committed during that period, he said.
He urged members of the House to extend cooperation to the investigators when they visit the districts.
He called on lawmakers to provide information on any police, former BDR or other law enforcement officials, or political activists, who were involved in, abetted or sheltered such crimes in their areas.
Seeking cooperation from all, the minister once again assured the House that such incidents would not be repeated.

item.title: Commerce minister: Bangladesh imports medicines from 72 countries, India tops list
item.description:
Bangladesh imports pharmaceutical products from 72 countries, with India topping the list as the largest source of imported medicines worth Tk1,227.40 crore in the fiscal year 2025-26, Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir told Parliament on Sunday.
He said this in a scripted reply to a question from opposition Jamaat-e-Islami lawmaker Md Abdul Gafur (Kushtia-2) in the House.
The minister placed a list of the top 20 countries from which Bangladesh imported the highest value of pharmaceutical products during the last fiscal year of 2025-2026.
According to the list, Bangladesh imported medicines worth Tk590.91 crore from France, Tk374.25 crore from China, Tk256.93 crore from Germany, Tk250.18 crore from Belgium, Tk234.33 crore from the United States and Tk224.09 crore from the Netherlands.
The other major sources included Switzerland (Tk165.50 crore), South Korea (Tk163.05 crore), Italy (Tk159.76 crore), Brazil (Tk159.60 crore), Hungary (Tk120.38 crore), Denmark (Tk93.02 crore), Spain (Tk79.51 crore), Portugal (Tk78.05 crore), the United Kingdom (Tk42.79 crore), Sweden (Tk38.11 crore), Turkey (Tk32.99 crore), Argentina (Tk30.14 crore) and Singapore (Tk23.43 crore).
In reply to another question from independent lawmaker Mohammad Salman Omer (Mymensingh-1), the commerce minister said Bangladesh exported pharmaceutical products worth $238.49 million during the fiscal year 2025-26.
He said Bangladeshi medicines were exported to a wide range of countries across Asia, Europe, Africa, the Americas and Oceania.
The minister also outlined several government initiatives to increase exports of pharmaceuticals and other products.
He said Bangladesh's export earnings remained heavily dependent on the readymade garment (RMG) sector, which accounts for 84% of the country's total export earnings.
To reduce dependence on a single export sector, the government has taken initiatives to extend facilities similar to those enjoyed by the RMG industry to other promising export sectors, he said.
Besides, bonded warehouse facilities have been extended to partially exporting companies in 18 sectors against bank guarantees, the minister said, adding that the National Board of Revenue (NBR) had already issued a government order in this regard.

item.title: Shama: India’s reported conditions for Hasina’s return have no legal basis
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam has dismissed reports that India has set conditions for the return of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, saying the reported demands have no basis in Bangladesh's laws.
Responding to reports that India had sought to ensure Hasina's right to appeal and restart her trial before agreeing to her return, Shama said Bangladesh had received no such proposal.
“No, not at all. We have had no such conversations with them on this matter,” she told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, referring to reports published by BBC Bangla.
She said Bangladesh expects Hasina, who has been sentenced to death for crimes against humanity, to be brought back from India under the existing extradition treaty.
“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has written to India multiple times under the extradition treaty,” she said, adding that the Ministries of Law and Home Affairs are examining the legal and technical aspects of the matter.
Shama said the government believes Hasina, like any other accused person, should be returned under the treaty to serve her sentence.
She also questioned whether Hasina's Bangladeshi citizenship alone would guarantee her the right to obtain a passport, saying the relevant laws do not require the government to issue passports to convicted criminals or individuals facing serious cases.
On bilateral relations, Shama said Bangladesh-India ties extend far beyond the issue of Hasina, emphasizing the longstanding relationship between the 2 neighboring countries and the importance of addressing bilateral matters through diplomacy.
“Bangladesh-India relations are a much bigger deal than Sheikh Hasina,” she said, urging against giving the issue more importance than necessary.
“We have issues. We will deal with the issues through diplomacy,” she said.
However, Shama said the government could not ignore Hasina's activities in India if they were aimed at destabilizing Bangladesh.
Regarding the Bangladesh-India Consular Dialogue, originally scheduled for November 17-18, Shama said the meeting had not been cancelled but deferred until a mutually convenient time.
She described reports of its cancellation as misinformation, saying both sides had agreed that it would be better to hold the talks later when they were available.
The state minister also indicated that Bangladesh would host several high-level foreign visits in the coming days, although she did not disclose any names or tentative dates.
Asked whether water-sharing issues, particularly the Ganges water issue, had been discussed at a meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Shama said the government could hold extensive discussions with the prime minister on a range of issues.
However, she did not directly confirm whether the Ganges water issue had been discussed at the meeting.

item.title: Law and order returns to normal in Gopalganj amid intensified joint patrols
item.description:
The law and order situation in Gopalganj has returned to normal following a period of violence and unrest.
With Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel deployed and joint forces intensifying patrols, government and private offices, courts and shops across the district reopened on Monday morning. Traffic movement also returned to normal on the Dhaka-Khulna highway and roads within the district town.
Additional police and BGB personnel remain deployed at key locations across the town to prevent further incidents, while joint force patrols continue.
On Sunday, the district witnessed protests, arson and vandalism. Leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned, and its affiliated organisations have been accused of orchestrating the violence.
During the unrest, the homes of several BNP leaders were vandalised, and a Grameen Bank branch was set on fire. BGB personnel were subsequently deployed to bring the situation under control.
Meanwhile, amid the developments, the officers-in-charge (OCs) of three police stations in the district were transferred on Sunday night.
The officers are Ayub Ali of Tungipara Police Station, Riad Mahmud of Kotalipara Police Station and Mahfuzur Rahman of Kashiani Police Station. All three have been transferred to Kishoreganj district.

item.title: Khasru: IMF loan talks to conclude by Jan-Feb’27
item.description:
Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury on Sunday said discussions with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on its new loan program are expected to conclude by January-February next year.
The government has no plan to withdraw from the IMF’s new loan program, but it is working to align the lender’s conditions and program with the country’s current economic realities and the government’s own five-year development plan, he said.
“Two working groups, one from each side, are working to resolve the differences with the IMF. The necessary adjustments will be made through discussions, after which the loan program will proceed in its normal course,” the minister said.
Khasru made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after inaugurating the two-day ‘International Debt Conference Bangladesh 2026’ at Hotel Ocean Paradise in Cox’s Bazar.
Prime Minister’s Special Assistant for Investment and Capital Market Tanvir Shahriar Ghani, Finance Secretary Md Khairuzzaman Mozumder, Financial Institutions Division Secretary Nazma Mobarek and senior officials of the Finance Ministry were present.
The finance minister said the government had no intention of ending its relationship with the IMF or discontinuing the loan program. Rather, it wants to implement the program in a manner consistent with the country’s economic realities, public interests and development priorities.
He said the agreement on the existing IMF loan program was reached during the tenure of the previous unelected government. The conditions agreed upon at that time could not be implemented overnight by the present elected government.
Sudden implementation of those conditions could put additional pressure on ordinary people and adversely affect businesses, trade and the overall economy, he added.
The government, therefore, wants to ensure adequate time and a gradual approach to implementing the IMF conditions, the minister said.
He noted that the government had already aligned its development plans with those of the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (Jica).
Similar discussions are now underway to bring the IMF program in line with the government’s priorities and plans.
The minister said a lack of coordination among development partners could create complications in project implementation. The government wants to advance their programs by taking into account the country’s priorities, institutional capacity and prevailing economic conditions.
He reiterated that the government’s position on continuing the IMF loan program was clear, although it was seeking necessary adjustments to the conditions in line with the country’s circumstances.
The two working groups are continuing discussions, and the government expects to complete the negotiations and coordination process by January-February next year. The program is expected to resume its normal pace following the completion of the discussions, he said.

item.title: Iran rules out UN inspections of damaged nuclear sites until war ends
item.description:
Iran will not let UN inspectors visit its damaged nuclear facilities until the Middle East war has ended and the United States meets its conditions, a senior Iranian official said.
The remarks came days after the International Atomic Energy Agency urged Tehran to take steps towards resuming inspections, which have been suspended since last year’s 12-day war with Israel, when the US also struck Iranian nuclear sites.
“We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran’s conditions are met and the war has permanently ended,” Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised interview late Sunday.
Iranian nuclear facilities were hit again during the Middle East war which broke out on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
IAEA inspectors visited Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant in September but have not gained access to other bombed sites including Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan.
Gharibabadi said the agency’s request to inspect damaged facilities was “likely aimed at assessing the effectiveness of American weaponry.”
Efforts to end the Middle East war have made little headway. Tehran is demanding that Washington unfreeze Iranian assets and lift sanctions, among other conditions, in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the vital energy shipping route it has blockaded during the conflict.
Iranian officials have said talks on Iran’s nuclear program would come at a later stage.
Earlier this month, the US military announced a $20 million reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program, a move Tehran called “repugnant.”

item.title: Bangladesh exports fruits worth $126.35m in FY26
item.description:
Bangladesh exported fruits worth $126.35 million in FY26, Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir told the parliament on Sunday.
“Bangladesh exports fruits to various international markets, including the United Arab Emirates, Austria, Australia, Bahrain, Canada, China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and the United States,” he said.
The minister said this while responding to a starred question from treasury bench member Md. Sadique Reaz (Dinajpur-2) during the day’s question-answer session in the House today with Deputy Speaker Barrister Kayser Kamal in the chair.
The minister said Bangladesh currently exports fruits to various countries and territories, including Austria, Bahrain, Germany, Denmark, France, Greece, Hong Kong, Ireland, Italy, Kuwait, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Oman, Poland, Portugal, Qatar, Sweden, Singapore and Vietnam.
Muktadir outlined several initiatives undertaken by the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) to expand exports of mangoes and other agricultural products.
He said the EPB organized a seminar titled “Export Opportunities and Diversification of Mango and Mango Products” in Chapainawabganj on October 19, 2023, to explore export potential, market expansion and diversification of mango and mango-based products.
The EPB also held a view exchange meeting with local mango growers, exporters and other stakeholders in Chapainawabganj on May 20, 2025, in presence of its vice-chairman, he added.
The minister said the EPB had provided comprehensive assistance to exporters in completing the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC) registration process to expand agricultural exports, particularly mango shipments, to China.
“Meridian Agro Industries Ltd. of Chattogram has secured GACC registration with the overall support of the Export Promotion Bureau,” he said.
He added that the EPB had also processed questionnaires submitted by Safe International Corporation and MTB Agro and Garden and forwarded them to the Commercial Counsellor at the Bangladesh Embassy in China on June 7, 2023.
Muktadir said the EPB vice-chairman inspected the Vapour Heat Treatment Plant in Gabtoli, Dhaka, on July 22, 2026, to assess the infrastructure and procedures required for agricultural exports.
An EPB meeting with all stakeholders was also held on August 10, 2026, to discuss exports of mangoes, jackfruits and other agricultural products to China and other international markets, GACC registration and ways to address existing barriers.
The minister said the EPB had taken initiatives to organize training programs involving the Department of Agricultural Extension, all stakeholders and exporters on GACC registration and registration procedures in other countries, phytosanitary requirements and export compliance.
The EPB also organized a training program for mango growers, farmers and stakeholders in Lama, Bandarban, on May 9, 2026.
The program covered mango production, disease and pest management, timely harvesting, grading and packaging, post-harvest management, vapour and hot water treatment, export procedures and marketing, he said.
The minister further said the EPB had undertaken a survey to assess the export potential of the country’s Geographical Indication (GI) products.
The survey will identify production capacity, product quality, international market demand, existing barriers, compliance requirements and potential export destinations for promising GI products. The EPB has finalised the terms of reference for appointing a survey firm, he added.
As part of efforts to promote and brand GI products and other promising agricultural goods in international markets, the EPB has included participation in six international trade fairs in its calendar for FY27.
The fairs include the 2026 Mekong-Lancang Fruits Festival in China’s Yunnan Province, the 22nd Malaysia International Halal Showcase (MIHAS) 2026, D-8 Halal Expo Indonesia 2026, Agro Food Jeddah 2026, the International Food and Drink Event and the International Halal Expo and World Halal Summit 2026.
The minister said these initiatives aimed to diversify agricultural exports, improve compliance with international standards and strengthen Bangladesh’s presence in global markets.

item.title: Govt plans to digitise all post offices by February 2028
item.description:
The government plans to transform all post offices across the country into digital service centres by February 2028 under two ongoing projects aimed at modernising postal services.
The initiatives will digitise the Postal Department’s financial services and introduce a national digital address database and route-mapping tool, the ‘Amar Dak’ app and the ‘Dak Bazar’ software.
Post, Telecommunications and Information Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam disclosed the plans on Monday while responding to a question from Rajshahi-5 MP Professor Nazrul Islam during the question-and-answer session on the sixth day of the fourth session of parliament.
The minister said a technical project titled “Sustainable and Modernisation of Mail Processing and Logistics Services” is being implemented from September 2024 to March 2027 to modernise postal operations and improve efficiency.
Another project, titled “Expansion and Accessibility of Existing Postal Services at Citizens’ Doorsteps”, is being implemented from March 2026 to February 2028.
Under the first project, the Postal Department’s existing electronic money transfer system is being upgraded to make it more modern and user-friendly.
The second project will digitise postal services through a national digital address database and route-mapping tool, the ‘Amar Dak’ app and the ‘Postal Rural Trade and Commerce Model’, known as ‘Dak Bazar’.
Once the projects are completed, all post offices will be transformed into digital service centres, allowing people across the country, including those in rural areas, to access secure digital postal services, the minister said.
Meanwhile, the minister outlined measures to prevent customer harassment, fraud and scams involving ‘Nagad’, the Postal Department’s digital financial service.
He said steps were being taken in line with directives from Bangladesh Bank, law enforcement agencies and the Directorate of Posts. Nagad provides round-the-clock customer support through its call centre at 16167, he said.
Currently, Nagad services are available at 97 post offices, while customer support is provided through a total of 113 service centres, including additional counters. Efforts are underway to gradually expand the network.
The minister said customers were regularly advised through awareness messages to keep their personal identification numbers (PINs) and one-time passwords (OTPs) confidential.
Suspicious transactions are also being monitored in coordination with relevant authorities to identify fraud networks.
Government allowances and other forms of assistance are now being transferred digitally and directly to beneficiaries’ accounts, he added.

item.title: Asean offers sidelined Myanmar leaders path back to talks
item.description:
Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Sunday to engage Myanmar’s government in stages, while making its return to high-level meetings conditional on progress on a regional peace plan.
Myanmar remains a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), but its political leaders have been barred from summits and foreign ministers’ meetings since October 2021.
The military seized power that year, overthrowing the elected government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi and triggering a civil war that continues today.
In a joint statement, the leaders called for “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground.”
They said Asean could gradually restore Myanmar’s full political representation if it makes “sustained and concrete progress” on the bloc’s five-point peace plan. The plan has yielded little since it was agreed on in 2021, and fighting continues between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups.
“What more can we do for Myanmar?” Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr asked at the leaders’ retreat in Manila. He urged the bloc to find practical ways to advance the peace plan and support an inclusive process led by Myanmar.
Thailand has pushed for closer engagement since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as civilian president this year following elections that monitors dismissed as a sham.
Leaders are also discussing trade, regional security and ways to share fuel supplies to cope with disruptions caused by the war in Iran. Australia and the Philippines signed a defense agreement on Sunday, while Canada and the Philippines announced on Saturday that they had concluded free trade negotiations.
A proposed code of conduct for the South China Sea remains unresolved. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said negotiations between Asean and China were 80% complete, but diplomats told AFP a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the summit.
US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive on Tuesday, toward the end of the summit, and meet the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other members of the Quad. The meeting is expected to precede talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.
Activists plan to march against Trump’s visit on Tuesday. Their protest is aimed in part at a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could displace Indigenous families.
The Philippines hands the rotating Asean chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due to take over in 2028.

item.title: COP31 faces deepening divides over climate finance, fossil fuel transition
item.description:
The final week of the UN climate summit COP31 opened on Monday with mounting pressure on governments to overcome divisions over climate finance, fossil fuel transition, adaptation and the rights of workers and vulnerable communities, as nearly 200 countries seek an agreement before the conference closes on November 20.
With more than 112 ministers expected to join high-level negotiations, the summit has entered a decisive phase. Australia is leading the negotiations while Türkiye holds the presidency, with both facing the challenge of translating existing climate commitments into measurable action.
At the heart of the negotiations is a widening divide between developed and developing countries over who should finance the global transition, how climate resources should be distributed and whether national energy pathways should be shaped by internationally agreed targets.
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has urged governments to avoid tactical delays and make progress on difficult issues.
The Australian-led negotiating process and Turkish presidency are working towards an overarching political declaration, known as the cover decision, intended to provide direction to the summit.
A proposed ministerial arrangement, called the Divan, will address five areas: adaptation, finance, mitigation, just transition and oceans.
However, negotiating blocs remain divided over the scope of the proposed declaration and its relationship with formal UN climate negotiations.
The Arab Group has opposed externally imposed sectoral targets and energy pathways that could undermine national priorities, while demanding that developed countries fulfil their financial commitments.
The African Group has stressed the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, warning that electrification targets without adequate financial and technological support could place additional burdens on developing economies.
Least Developed Countries are demanding stronger adaptation measures, replenishment of climate funds and progress on implementing the first Global Stocktake, including support through the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.
One of Türkiye's major initiatives, the 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption from around 23% to 35% by 2035. More than 30 countries have backed the initiative.
The pledge promotes electrification across transport, buildings and industry, but its climate benefits will depend on the sources of electricity and investment in renewable energy, transmission networks and storage.
The target does not mean generating 35% of electricity from renewable sources. Without a parallel expansion of clean energy, growing electricity demand could also be met through fossil fuel generation.
The European Union wants COP31 to reinforce implementation of the first Global Stocktake and the transition away from fossil fuels.
However, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra has cautioned against making an absolute clean-energy condition compulsory for participation in the electrification initiative.
China has also called for pragmatism and consensus while promoting renewable energy cooperation and investment.
Meanwhile, environmental and human rights organisations have warned that electrification without social and environmental safeguards could intensify pressure on communities affected by critical mineral extraction.
The debate has gained further significance as Türkiye promotes electrification while announcing new oil exploration activities.
Climate finance remains one of the most contentious issues at COP31, with developing countries demanding predictable, accessible and predominantly grant-based funding.
Under the COP29 agreement, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035. The broader ambition is to scale up climate finance from all sources to at least $1.3 trillion annually by the same year.
However, a report presented by Brazil's COP30 presidency estimated that climate finance could reach only $458 billion-$461 billion annually by 2035 under a business-as-usual scenario, leaving a projected gap of approximately $840 billion against the $1.3 trillion ambition.
Stronger policy interventions could potentially increase annual finance flows to between $1.27 trillion and $1.41 trillion, according to the report.
Developing countries argue that private investment and loans cannot replace the financial obligations of developed countries under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement.
They also warn that loans on unfavourable terms could deepen debt burdens in economies already struggling with climate impacts and limited fiscal resources.
At a ministerial dialogue, Stiell highlighted the need to reduce the cost of capital, simplify access to finance and make funding more responsive to vulnerable economies.
The dispute over climate finance extends to adaptation and the growing costs of climate-related destruction.
The African Group is pushing for a tripling of adaptation finance, while civil society organisations have called for at least $120 billion annually well before 2035, with public grants playing a central role.
One negotiating proposal involves increasing adaptation finance from an estimated $40 billion baseline in 2025 to $120 billion by 2035. However, this remains under discussion rather than an agreed commitment.
The Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage is also facing pressure to accelerate financial support.
Estimates by the Loss and Damage Collaboration put annual needs in developing countries at more than $724 billion. Meanwhile, requests amounting to approximately $2.8 billion have been made against an available funding envelope of around $342 million.
For countries such as Bangladesh, these financing gaps have immediate consequences. River erosion, flooding, salinity intrusion, displacement and infrastructure damage threaten livelihoods, public services and development gains.
The Just Transition Work Programme has emerged as another major negotiating challenge.
Countries broadly support a fair transition towards low-emission and climate-resilient economies but disagree over financing, governance and the establishment of a permanent Belém Action Mechanism under the UN climate process.
Civil society organisations and worker representatives want workers, women, young people, Indigenous Peoples, informal waste workers and affected communities to have meaningful roles in decision-making.
The debate extends beyond fossil fuel industries to agriculture, fisheries, transport and manufacturing, where changing energy systems and climate policies could reshape employment and livelihoods.
Gender negotiations have also exposed differences, although countries have adopted conclusions on the first year of the Belém Gender Action Plan for 2026–2034.
For Bangladesh, the negotiations carry significant implications for implementing its third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0).
Achieving national climate targets will require substantial investment, institutional coordination, technical capacity and international support.
A just transition must also protect farmers, fishers, industrial workers, women, young people and communities facing displacement.
Meaningful participation, predictable grant-based finance, skills development, stronger social protection and transparent accountability will be essential to ensure that climate commitments translate into tangible benefits.
Beyond formal negotiations, COP31's Action Agenda is highlighting investment initiatives in electricity grids, clean energy, zero-emission freight and methane reduction.
A memorandum involving British International Investment, Norway's Norfund and FinDev Canada under the 10by30 initiative aims to support at least $10 billion in climate investment activity over five years to 2030.
Six UN agencies have also launched a platform seeking to improve access to more than $3 billion in disaster risk financing by 2030, with the aim of protecting 75 million people and their livelihoods.
However, these announcements represent different types of investment commitments and initiatives, not necessarily new funding pledged at COP31 or money already disbursed.
For developing countries, the credibility of these initiatives will depend on whether announced investments become accessible finance and deliver measurable benefits to vulnerable communities.
The urgency of the negotiations is reinforced by the UN Environment Programme's Emissions Gap Report 2026, which projects approximately 2.8°C of global warming by 2100 under current policies.
Full implementation of existing national climate commitments would reduce the projection to around 2.6°C, still significantly above the Paris Agreement's temperature goals.
The report says the world has already lost the opportunity to avoid temporarily exceeding the 1.5°C threshold. The priority now is to minimise the scale and duration of the overshoot and establish a credible pathway back to 1.5°C.
Under the lowest-overshoot pathway assessed by UNEP, global greenhouse gas emissions would need to fall by 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
As COP31 approaches its November 20 conclusion, the international community faces a fundamental test: whether governments can move beyond political declarations and investment announcements to deliver the finance, technology and cooperation needed for climate action.
For developing countries, the outcome must address historical responsibility, financial inequality, adaptation needs and the protection of communities already experiencing the consequences of climate change.
Ultimately, COP31's success will be measured not by the number of pledges announced in Antalya, but by whether its decisions translate into real action for people and countries on the frontline of the climate crisis.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: Death-row convict found hanging in Kashimpur prison
item.description:
A death-row convict in two murder cases was found hanging inside Kashimpur High-Security Central Prison in Gazipur early Monday.
The deceased, Farhad, 41, was the son of the late Hafiz Uddin of Shalinapara village in Tangail Sadar upazila.
Senior Jail Superintendent Mohammad Abdullah-Al-Mamun confirmed the incident, saying Farhad's body was discovered at around 1am in a ground-floor cell of the prison's Himel Building.
He said prison authorities had completed a routine headcount on Sunday before locking the cells for the night. Farhad, who had been sentenced to death for the murder of a man and a woman in Tangail, was sharing the cell with two co-accused.
During the night, the two inmates found him hanging from a cell window with a towel tied around his neck, the superintendent said.
Prison officials were alerted, recovered Farhad and rushed him to Gazipur Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead on arrival.
An inquest has been conducted, and the body will be handed over to the family after an autopsy, he added. Relatives have arrived at the prison.
The superintendent said Farhad was transferred to Kashimpur High-Security Prison from Dhaka Central Jail in Keraniganj on August 26, 2019.
He was being held in connection with two separate murder cases filed with Tangail police station, in which he had received death sentences.
Abdullah-Al-Mamun also said Farhad had been suffering from various health problems, including severe headaches and visual hallucinations, for around a year. He had received medical treatment at the prison hospital several times.

item.title: Chinmoy Krishna shifted from Chittagong jail to Keraniganj special prison
item.description:
Chinmoy Krishna Das Brahmachari, spokesperson for the Sanatani Jagaran Jote, has been transferred from Chittagong Central Jail to a special prison in Keraniganj, Dhaka.
He was transferred under tight security at around 5am on Monday (November 16), Chittagong Central Jail Senior Jail Superintendent Iqbal Hossain confirmed to Dhaka Tribune.
“Chinmoy Krishna Das has been taken to the special prison in Keraniganj, Dhaka,” he said, adding that he could not provide further details about the reasons for the sudden transfer.
Prison sources said Ranganath Das Brahmachari, who prepares meals for Chinmoy, was not transferred with him and remains at Chittagong Central Jail.
On October 31, 2024, Firoz Khan, then general secretary of the BNP's Mohra Ward unit in Chandgaon, filed a sedition case with Kotwali police against Chinmoy Krishna Das and 18 others over allegations of disrespecting the national flag.
Chinmoy was arrested in Dhaka on November 25, 2024, in connection with the case.
The following day, a Chittagong court rejected his bail petition and ordered him sent to jail. His supporters subsequently surrounded the prison van and staged protests on the court premises. Police fired sound grenades to disperse them before taking him to jail.
During the unrest, several motorcycles and vehicles were vandalised near the court. Later, lawyer Saiful Islam Alif was hacked and beaten to death near Rangam Convention Hall, allegedly by supporters of Chinmoy.
On November 29, 2024, Alif's father, Jamal Uddin, filed a murder case with Kotwali Police Station. The case statement named 31 people and accused another 15 to 16 unidentified individuals.
After completing the investigation, Assistant Commissioner of Chittagong Metropolitan Police (Kotwali) Mahfuzur Rahman submitted a charge sheet on July 1, 2025, naming 38 people as accused. Chinmoy Krishna Das was named as the prime accused.

item.title: Bangladesh’s largest solar power plant expected to begin operations in June 2028
item.description:
Electricity Generation Bangladesh (EGB) is constructing the country's largest solar power plant with a capacity of 220 megawatts (MW) in Sonagazi, Feni, at an estimated cost of Tk 1,888.10 crore, with plans to complete the project by June 30, 2028.
State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Anindya Islam Amit inaugurated a start-up workshop on the project on Monday.
Speaking at the event, the state minister said the government aims to meet 20 percent of the country’s electricity demand from renewable energy sources by 2030. "Our target is to generate 10,000 megawatts of electricity from renewable sources by 2030. The government has formulated supportive policies in this regard," he said, adding that the Sonagazi 220MW solar project will play an important role in achieving that goal.
According to a press release, the project is being implemented under joint financing from the Bangladesh government, the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), and EGB's own funds. A financing agreement between the Economic Relations Division (ERD) and IsDB was signed on August 3.
Once operational, the plant is expected to supply around 441.18 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of electricity annually to the national grid starting in June 2028, contributing significantly to the government's target of generating 10,000MW from solar energy by 2030.
Under the project, around 469,560 solar photovoltaic (PV) modules, 26 inverters, and two substations will be installed. There are also plans to introduce an agrivoltaic concept to allow agricultural activities and livestock rearing alongside solar power generation on the same land.
Additionally, the project includes initiatives to provide skill development training for about 1,000 local unemployed youths and women, set up computer labs, and install rooftop solar panels at local educational institutions.
Meanwhile, the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) approved a project on September 29 to acquire 386 acres of land for building another 130MW solar power plant in Sonagazi. Alongside this, there is a plan to construct a 150MW floating solar power plant at Muchapur. Once implemented, these initiatives could transform the area into a major solar power hub with a combined capacity of around 600MW.
EGB believes the project is not merely an initiative to boost electricity generation, but will also play a vital role in promoting clean energy, environmental protection, local employment, and sustainable socio-economic development.
Power Division Secretary Mirana Mahrook, IsDB Dhaka Regional Hub Resident Head Ali M. Khan, Operational Team Leader Nasser Mohammed Yakubu, EGB Chairman K. M. Ali Reza, Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) Chairman Md. Rezaul Karim, and EGB Managing Director A K M Manjur Kadir, among other officials, attended the workshop.
